# iddqd 0.4.5 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/iddqd/0.4.5

# iddqd

Maps where keys are borrowed from values.

This crate consists of several map types, collectively called **ID maps**:

- `IdOrdMap`
- `IdHashMap`
- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

## Usage

- Pick your ID map type.
- Depending on the ID map type, implement `IdOrdItem``IdHashItem``BiHashItem``TriHashItem`
- Store values in the ID map type.

### Features

This crate was built out a practical need for map types, and addresses issues encountered using Rust’s default map types in practice at Oxide.

- Keys are retrieved from values, not stored separately from them. Separate storage has been a recurring pain point in our codebases: if keys are duplicated within values, it’s proven to be hard to maintain consistency between keys and values. This crate addresses that need.
- Keys may be borrowed from values, which allows for more flexible implementations. (They don’t have to be borrowed, but they can be.)
- There’s no `insert`method; insertion must be through either`insert_overwrite`or`insert_unique`. You must pick an insertion behavior.
- For hash maps, the default hasher is `foldhash`*not provide the same level of HashDoS resistance*as SipHash. If that is important to you, you can use a different hasher. (Disable the`default-hasher`feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed in.)
- The serde implementations reject duplicate keys.

We’ve also sometimes needed to index a set of data by more than one key, or
perhaps map one key to another. For that purpose, this crate provides
[ BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.5/iddqd/bi_hash_map/imp/struct.BiHashMap.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.5/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp/struct.TriHashMap.html)

`TriHashMap`- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

As a consequence of the general API structure, maps can have arbitrary non-key data associated with them as well.

### Examples

An example for [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.5/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html):

```
use ;
// Implement IdOrdItem so the map knows how to get the key from the value.
let mut users = new;
// You must pick an insertion behavior. insert_unique returns an error if
// the key already exists.
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
// Lookup by name:
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// Iterate over users:
for user in &users
```
Keys don’t have to be borrowed from the value. For smaller `Copy` types,
it’s recommended that you use owned keys. Here’s an example of using
[ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.5/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) with a small integer key:

```
// ...
```
An example for [ IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.5/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp/struct.IdHashMap.html), showing a complex borrowed key. Here,
“complex” means that the key is not a reference itself, but a struct that
returns references to more than one field from the value.

```
use ;
// The key type is a borrowed form of the name and version. It needs to
// implement `Eq + Hash`.
// Create a new `IdHashMap` with the given artifacts. This uses the
// `id_hash_map!` macro that comes with iddqd.
let artifacts = id_hash_map! ;
// Look up artifacts by name and version.
assert_eq!;
```
For more examples, see the
[examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd/examples)
and [extended
examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples)
directories.

`Equivalent` and `Comparable`

An important feature of the standard library’s maps is that they allow any
borrowed form of the key type to be used for lookups; for example, a
`HashMap<String, T>` type can be looked up with a `&str` key. This is done
through the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait.

But the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait is a bit too restrictive for complex keys such as

`ArtifactKey` above, requiring workarounds such as [dynamic dispatch](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example). To address this, the crates.io ecosystem has standardized on the

[and](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html)

`Equivalent`[traits as generalizations of](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable``Borrow`. The map types in
this crate require these traits.For a key type `T::Key<'_>` and a query type `Q`:

- The hash map types require `Q: Hash + Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. Also,`Q`must hash in the same way as`T::Key<'_>`. Typically, this is done by ensuring that enum variants and struct fields are in the same order[^proptest].
- `IdOrdMap`- `Q: Comparable<T::Key<'_>>`, which in turn requires- `Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. (There’s no need for- `Q`to implement- `Ord`or- `Eq`itself.)

[^proptest]: We recommend that you test this with e.g. a property-based
test: see [this
example](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example/blob/a6f17699/src/lib.rs#L233).

Continuing the `ArtifactKey` example from above, we can perform a lookup
using a key of this owned form:

```
use Equivalent;
// This is an owned form of ArtifactKey. The fields are in the same
// order as ArtifactKey's fields, so it hashes the same way.
// Now you can use OwnedArtifactKey to look up the artifact.
let owned_key = OwnedArtifactKey ;
assert_eq!;
```
There’s a blanket implementation of [ Equivalent](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html) and

[for](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable`[, so if your type already implements](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`[, there aren’t any extra steps to take.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`## Testing and verification

This crate is validated through a combination of:

- Unit tests
- Property-based tests using a naive map as an oracle
- Unit and property-based tests for several kinds of pathological `Eq`,`Hash`and`Ord`implementations
- Property-based tests for panic safety
- Miri tests for unsafe code, checked against both Stacked and Tree Borrows
- Compile-fail UI tests to ensure invalid patterns are rejected by the borrow checker
- Bounded formal verification for core invariants and UB using
[Soteria](https://soteria-tools.com)

Pathological user implementations written in safe Rust might corrupt internal map state and result in panics, but should never cause UB.

For more information on our validation philosophy, see [this Oxide blog
entry](https://oxide.computer/blog/iddqd-unsafe).

If you see a gap in testing, new tests are welcome. Thank you!

Note that **testing requires  cargo-nextest**: several
tests depend on nextest’s process-per-test model.

## No-std compatibility

Most of this crate is no-std compatible, though [ alloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/index.html) is required.

The [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.5/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) type is not currently no-std compatible due to its use of a
thread-local. This thread-local is just a way to work around a limitation in
std’s

`BTreeMap` API, though. Either a custom B-Tree implementation, or a
platform-specific notion of thread locals, would suffice to make
[no-std compatible.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.5/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html)

`IdOrdMap`## Optional features

- `allocator-api2`: Enables support for custom allocators via the- `allocator_api2`- `bumpalo`) are supported. Custom allocators are not currently supported by- `IdOrdMap`.
- `daft`: Enables- `daft`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `default-hasher`: Enables the- `DefaultHashBuilder`type. Disable this feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed into- `IdHashMap`- `BiHashMap`- `TriHashMap`- *Enabled by default.*
- `proptest`: Enables- `proptest`- `Arbitrary`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `schemars08`: Enables- `schemars`- [automatic replacement](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/blob/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples/typify-types.rs)through- `typify`- `dropshot`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `serde`: Enables serde support for all ID map types.- *Not enabled by default.*
- `std`: Enables std support.- *Enabled by default.*

## Related work

-
`bimap`
-
`multi_index_map``Clone`. In`iddqd`, we pick a somewhat different point in the design space, but we think`multi_index_map`is also great.
-
In general, this is similar to relational database records with indexes. For sufficiently complex use cases, consider an embedded database like [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/), or even a networked database like[PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/).`iddqd`is a good fit for simple in-memory caches of data stored in these databases.

## Minimum supported Rust version (MSRV)

This crate’s MSRV is **Rust 1.85**. In general we aim for 6 months of Rust
compatibility.

## What does iddqd mean?

The name `iddqd` is a reference to [a cheat
code](https://doomwiki.org/wiki/Doom_cheat_codes) in the classic video game
*Doom*. It has `id` in the name, and is short and memorable.

# iddqd - Rust

## Expand description

This crate consists of several map types, collectively called **ID maps**:

- `IdOrdMap`
- `IdHashMap`
- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

- Pick your ID map type.
- Depending on the ID map type, implement `IdOrdItem``IdHashItem``BiHashItem``TriHashItem`
- Store values in the ID map type.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

This crate was built out a practical need for map types, and addresses issues encountered using Rust’s default map types in practice at Oxide.

- Keys are retrieved from values, not stored separately from them. Separate storage has been a recurring pain point in our codebases: if keys are duplicated within values, it’s proven to be hard to maintain consistency between keys and values. This crate addresses that need.
- Keys may be borrowed from values, which allows for more flexible implementations. (They don’t have to be borrowed, but they can be.)
- There’s no `insert`method; insertion must be through either`insert_overwrite`or`insert_unique`. You must pick an insertion behavior.
- For hash maps, the default hasher is `foldhash`*not provide the same level of HashDoS resistance*as SipHash. If that is important to you, you can use a different hasher. (Disable the`default-hasher`feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed in.)
- The serde implementations reject duplicate keys.

We’ve also sometimes needed to index a set of data by more than one key, or
perhaps map one key to another. For that purpose, this crate provides
[ BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.BiHashMap.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.TriHashMap.html)

`TriHashMap`- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

As a consequence of the general API structure, maps can have arbitrary non-key data associated with them as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

An example for [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdOrdMap.html):

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug)]
struct User {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
}
// Implement IdOrdItem so the map knows how to get the key from the value.
impl IdOrdItem for User {
    // The key type can borrow from the value.
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut users = IdOrdMap::<User>::new();
// You must pick an insertion behavior. insert_unique returns an error if
// the key already exists.
users.insert_unique(User { name: "Alice".to_string(), age: 30 }).unwrap();
users.insert_unique(User { name: "Bob".to_string(), age: 35 }).unwrap();
// Lookup by name:
assert_eq!(users.get("Alice").unwrap().age, 30);
assert_eq!(users.get("Bob").unwrap().age, 35);
// Iterate over users:
for user in &users {
    println!("User {}: {}", user.name, user.age);
}
```
Keys don’t have to be borrowed from the value. For smaller `Copy` types,
it’s recommended that you use owned keys. Here’s an example of using
[ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdOrdMap.html) with a small integer key:

```
struct Record {
    id: u32,
    data: String,
}
impl IdOrdItem for Record {
    // The key type is small, so an owned key is preferred.
    type Key<'a> = u32;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
// ...
```
An example for [ IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdHashMap.html), showing a complex borrowed key. Here,
“complex” means that the key is not a reference itself, but a struct that
returns references to more than one field from the value.

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, id_hash_map, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Artifact {
    name: String,
    version: String,
    data: Vec<u8>,
}
// The key type is a borrowed form of the name and version. It needs to
// implement `Eq + Hash`.
#[derive(Eq, Hash, PartialEq)]
struct ArtifactKey<'a> {
    name: &'a str,
    version: &'a str,
}
impl IdHashItem for Artifact {
    // The key type can borrow from the value.
    type Key<'a> = ArtifactKey<'a>;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        ArtifactKey { name: &self.name, version: &self.version }
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
// Create a new `IdHashMap` with the given artifacts. This uses the
// `id_hash_map!` macro that comes with iddqd.
let artifacts = id_hash_map! {
    Artifact {
        name: "artifact1".to_owned(),
        version: "1.0".to_owned(),
        data: b"data1".to_vec(),
    },
    Artifact {
        name: "artifact2".to_owned(),
        version: "1.0".to_owned(),
        data: b"data2".to_vec(),
    },
};
// Look up artifacts by name and version.
assert_eq!(
    artifacts
        .get(&ArtifactKey { name: "artifact1", version: "1.0" })
        .unwrap()
        .data,
    b"data1",
);
```
For more examples, see the
[examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd/examples)
and [extended
examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples)
directories.

[§](https://docs.rs#equivalent-and-comparable)`Equivalent` and `Comparable`

An important feature of the standard library’s maps is that they allow any
borrowed form of the key type to be used for lookups; for example, a
`HashMap<String, T>` type can be looked up with a `&str` key. This is done
through the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait.

But the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait is a bit too restrictive for complex keys such as

`ArtifactKey` above, requiring workarounds such as [dynamic dispatch](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example). To address this, the crates.io ecosystem has standardized on the

[and](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html)

`Equivalent`[traits as generalizations of](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable``Borrow`. The map types in
this crate require these traits.For a key type `T::Key<'_>` and a query type `Q`:

- The hash map types require `Q: Hash + Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. Also,`Q`must hash in the same way as`T::Key<'_>`. Typically, this is done by ensuring that enum variants and struct fields are in the same order[1](https://docs.rs#fn1)
- `IdOrdMap`- `Q: Comparable<T::Key<'_>>`, which in turn requires- `Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. (There’s no need for- `Q`to implement- `Ord`or- `Eq`itself.)

Continuing the `ArtifactKey` example from above, we can perform a lookup
using a key of this owned form:

```
use equivalent::Equivalent;
// This is an owned form of ArtifactKey. The fields are in the same
// order as ArtifactKey's fields, so it hashes the same way.
#[derive(Hash)]
struct OwnedArtifactKey {
    name: String,
    version: String,
}
impl Equivalent<ArtifactKey<'_>> for OwnedArtifactKey {
    fn equivalent(&self, other: &ArtifactKey<'_>) -> bool {
        self.name == other.name && self.version == other.version
    }
}
// Now you can use OwnedArtifactKey to look up the artifact.
let owned_key = OwnedArtifactKey {
    name: "artifact1".to_owned(),
    version: "1.0".to_owned(),
};
assert_eq!(artifacts.get(&owned_key).unwrap().data, b"data1",);
```
There’s a blanket implementation of [ Equivalent](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html) and

[for](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable`[, so if your type already implements](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`[, there aren’t any extra steps to take.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

# iddqd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.5/iddqd/index.html

## Expand description

Maps where keys are borrowed from values.

This crate consists of several map types, collectively called **ID maps**:

- `IdOrdMap`
- `IdHashMap`
- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

- Pick your ID map type.
- Depending on the ID map type, implement `IdOrdItem``IdHashItem``BiHashItem``TriHashItem`
- Store values in the ID map type.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

This crate was built out a practical need for map types, and addresses issues encountered using Rust’s default map types in practice at Oxide.

- Keys are retrieved from values, not stored separately from them. Separate storage has been a recurring pain point in our codebases: if keys are duplicated within values, it’s proven to be hard to maintain consistency between keys and values. This crate addresses that need.
- Keys may be borrowed from values, which allows for more flexible implementations. (They don’t have to be borrowed, but they can be.)
- There’s no `insert`method; insertion must be through either`insert_overwrite`or`insert_unique`. You must pick an insertion behavior.
- For hash maps, the default hasher is `foldhash`*not provide the same level of HashDoS resistance*as SipHash. If that is important to you, you can use a different hasher. (Disable the`default-hasher`feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed in.)
- The serde implementations reject duplicate keys.

We’ve also sometimes needed to index a set of data by more than one key, or
perhaps map one key to another. For that purpose, this crate provides
[ BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.BiHashMap.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.TriHashMap.html)

`TriHashMap`- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

As a consequence of the general API structure, maps can have arbitrary non-key data associated with them as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

An example for [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdOrdMap.html):

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug)]
struct User {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
}
// Implement IdOrdItem so the map knows how to get the key from the value.
impl IdOrdItem for User {
    // The key type can borrow from the value.
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut users = IdOrdMap::<User>::new();
// You must pick an insertion behavior. insert_unique returns an error if
// the key already exists.
users.insert_unique(User { name: "Alice".to_string(), age: 30 }).unwrap();
users.insert_unique(User { name: "Bob".to_string(), age: 35 }).unwrap();
// Lookup by name:
assert_eq!(users.get("Alice").unwrap().age, 30);
assert_eq!(users.get("Bob").unwrap().age, 35);
// Iterate over users:
for user in &users {
    println!("User {}: {}", user.name, user.age);
}
```
Keys don’t have to be borrowed from the value. For smaller `Copy` types,
it’s recommended that you use owned keys. Here’s an example of using
[ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdOrdMap.html) with a small integer key:

```
struct Record {
    id: u32,
    data: String,
}
impl IdOrdItem for Record {
    // The key type is small, so an owned key is preferred.
    type Key<'a> = u32;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
// ...
```
An example for [ IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdHashMap.html), showing a complex borrowed key. Here,
“complex” means that the key is not a reference itself, but a struct that
returns references to more than one field from the value.

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, id_hash_map, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Artifact {
    name: String,
    version: String,
    data: Vec<u8>,
}
// The key type is a borrowed form of the name and version. It needs to
// implement `Eq + Hash`.
#[derive(Eq, Hash, PartialEq)]
struct ArtifactKey<'a> {
    name: &'a str,
    version: &'a str,
}
impl IdHashItem for Artifact {
    // The key type can borrow from the value.
    type Key<'a> = ArtifactKey<'a>;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        ArtifactKey { name: &self.name, version: &self.version }
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
// Create a new `IdHashMap` with the given artifacts. This uses the
// `id_hash_map!` macro that comes with iddqd.
let artifacts = id_hash_map! {
    Artifact {
        name: "artifact1".to_owned(),
        version: "1.0".to_owned(),
        data: b"data1".to_vec(),
    },
    Artifact {
        name: "artifact2".to_owned(),
        version: "1.0".to_owned(),
        data: b"data2".to_vec(),
    },
};
// Look up artifacts by name and version.
assert_eq!(
    artifacts
        .get(&ArtifactKey { name: "artifact1", version: "1.0" })
        .unwrap()
        .data,
    b"data1",
);
```
For more examples, see the
[examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd/examples)
and [extended
examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples)
directories.

[§](https://docs.rs#equivalent-and-comparable)`Equivalent` and `Comparable`

An important feature of the standard library’s maps is that they allow any
borrowed form of the key type to be used for lookups; for example, a
`HashMap<String, T>` type can be looked up with a `&str` key. This is done
through the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait.

But the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait is a bit too restrictive for complex keys such as

`ArtifactKey` above, requiring workarounds such as [dynamic dispatch](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example). To address this, the crates.io ecosystem has standardized on the

[and](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html)

`Equivalent`[traits as generalizations of](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable``Borrow`. The map types in
this crate require these traits.For a key type `T::Key<'_>` and a query type `Q`:

- The hash map types require `Q: Hash + Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. Also,`Q`must hash in the same way as`T::Key<'_>`. Typically, this is done by ensuring that enum variants and struct fields are in the same order[1](https://docs.rs#fn1)
- `IdOrdMap`- `Q: Comparable<T::Key<'_>>`, which in turn requires- `Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. (There’s no need for- `Q`to implement- `Ord`or- `Eq`itself.)

Continuing the `ArtifactKey` example from above, we can perform a lookup
using a key of this owned form:

```
use equivalent::Equivalent;
// This is an owned form of ArtifactKey. The fields are in the same
// order as ArtifactKey's fields, so it hashes the same way.
#[derive(Hash)]
struct OwnedArtifactKey {
    name: String,
    version: String,
}
impl Equivalent<ArtifactKey<'_>> for OwnedArtifactKey {
    fn equivalent(&self, other: &ArtifactKey<'_>) -> bool {
        self.name == other.name && self.version == other.version
    }
}
// Now you can use OwnedArtifactKey to look up the artifact.
let owned_key = OwnedArtifactKey {
    name: "artifact1".to_owned(),
    version: "1.0".to_owned(),
};
assert_eq!(artifacts.get(&owned_key).unwrap().data, b"data1",);
```
There’s a blanket implementation of [ Equivalent](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html) and

[for](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable`[, so if your type already implements](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`[, there aren’t any extra steps to take.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`[§](https://docs.rs#testing-and-verification)Testing and verification

This crate is validated through a combination of:

- Unit tests
- Property-based tests using a naive map as an oracle
- Unit and property-based tests for several kinds of pathological `Eq`,`Hash`and`Ord`implementations
- Property-based tests for panic safety
- Miri tests for unsafe code, checked against both Stacked and Tree Borrows
- Compile-fail UI tests to ensure invalid patterns are rejected by the borrow checker
- Bounded formal verification for core invariants and UB using
[Soteria](https://soteria-tools.com)

Pathological user implementations written in safe Rust might corrupt internal map state and result in panics, but should never cause UB.

For more information on our validation philosophy, see [this Oxide blog
entry](https://oxide.computer/blog/iddqd-unsafe).

If you see a gap in testing, new tests are welcome. Thank you!

Note that **testing requires  cargo-nextest**: several
tests depend on nextest’s process-per-test model.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-compatibility)No-std compatibility

Most of this crate is no-std compatible, though [ alloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/index.html) is required.

The [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdOrdMap.html) type is not currently no-std compatible due to its use of a
thread-local. This thread-local is just a way to work around a limitation in
std’s

`BTreeMap` API, though. Either a custom B-Tree implementation, or a
platform-specific notion of thread locals, would suffice to make
[no-std compatible.](https://docs.rs/struct.IdOrdMap.html)

`IdOrdMap`[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

- `allocator-api2`: Enables support for custom allocators via the- `allocator_api2`- `bumpalo`) are supported. Custom allocators are not currently supported by- `IdOrdMap`.
- `daft`: Enables- `daft`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `default-hasher`: Enables the- `DefaultHashBuilder`type. Disable this feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed into- `IdHashMap`- `BiHashMap`- `TriHashMap`- *Enabled by default.*
- `proptest`: Enables- `proptest`- `Arbitrary`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `schemars08`: Enables- `schemars`- [automatic replacement](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/blob/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples/typify-types.rs)through- `typify`- `dropshot`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `serde`: Enables serde support for all ID map types.- *Not enabled by default.*
- `std`: Enables std support.- *Enabled by default.*

[§](https://docs.rs#related-work)Related work

-
`bimap`
-
`multi_index_map``Clone`. In`iddqd`, we pick a somewhat different point in the design space, but we think`multi_index_map`is also great.
-
In general, this is similar to relational database records with indexes. For sufficiently complex use cases, consider an embedded database like [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/), or even a networked database like[PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/).`iddqd`is a good fit for simple in-memory caches of data stored in these databases.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version-msrv)Minimum supported Rust version (MSRV)

This crate’s MSRV is **Rust 1.85**. In general we aim for 6 months of Rust
compatibility.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-does-iddqd-mean)What does iddqd mean?

The name `iddqd` is a reference to [a cheat
code](https://doomwiki.org/wiki/Doom_cheat_codes) in the classic video game
*Doom*. It has `id` in the name, and is short and memorable.

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.5/src/iddqd/lib.rs.html

# iddqd/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! Maps where keys are borrowed from values.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! This crate consists of several map types, collectively called **ID maps**:
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! - [`IdOrdMap`]: A B-Tree based map where keys are borrowed from values.
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! - [`IdHashMap`]: A hash map where keys are borrowed from values.
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! - [`BiHashMap`]: A bijective (1:1) hash map with two keys, borrowed from
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!   values.
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! - [`TriHashMap`]: A trijective (1:1:1) hash map with three keys, borrowed
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!   from values.
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! # Usage
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! * Pick your ID map type.
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! * Depending on the ID map type, implement [`IdOrdItem`], [`IdHashItem`],
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!   [`BiHashItem`], or [`TriHashItem`] for your value type.
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! * Store values in the ID map type.
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! ## Features
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! This crate was built out a practical need for map types, and addresses
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! issues encountered using Rust's default map types in practice at Oxide.
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! * Keys are retrieved from values, not stored separately from them. Separate
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!   storage has been a recurring pain point in our codebases: if keys are
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!   duplicated within values, it's proven to be hard to maintain consistency
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!   between keys and values. This crate addresses that need.
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! * Keys may be borrowed from values, which allows for more flexible
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!   implementations. (They don't have to be borrowed, but they can be.)
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! * There's no `insert` method; insertion must be through either
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!   `insert_overwrite` or `insert_unique`. You must pick an insertion
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!   behavior.
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! * For hash maps, the default hasher is [`foldhash`], which is much faster
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!   than SipHash. However, foldhash does *not provide the same level of HashDoS
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!   resistance* as SipHash. If that is important to you, you can use a different
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!   hasher. (Disable the `default-hasher` feature to require a hash
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!   builder type parameter to be passed in.)
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! * The serde implementations reject duplicate keys.
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! We've also sometimes needed to index a set of data by more than one key, or
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! perhaps map one key to another. For that purpose, this crate provides
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! [`BiHashMap`] and [`TriHashMap`].
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! * [`BiHashMap`] has two keys, and provides a bijection (1:1 relationship)
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!   between the keys.
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! * [`TriHashMap`] has three keys, and provides a trijection (1:1:1
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!   relationship) between the keys.
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! As a consequence of the general API structure, maps can have arbitrary
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! non-key data associated with them as well.
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! ## Examples
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! An example for [`IdOrdMap`]:
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! ```
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! # #[cfg(feature = "std")] {
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! #[derive(Debug)]
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! struct User {
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!     name: String,
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!     age: u8,
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! }
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! // Implement IdOrdItem so the map knows how to get the key from the value.
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! impl IdOrdItem for User {
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!     // The key type can borrow from the value.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!     type Key<'a> = &'a str;
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!     fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!         &self.name
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!     }
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!     id_upcast!();
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! }
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! let mut users = IdOrdMap::<User>::new();
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! // You must pick an insertion behavior. insert_unique returns an error if
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! // the key already exists.
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! users.insert_unique(User { name: "Alice".to_string(), age: 30 }).unwrap();
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! users.insert_unique(User { name: "Bob".to_string(), age: 35 }).unwrap();
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! // Lookup by name:
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! assert_eq!(users.get("Alice").unwrap().age, 30);
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! assert_eq!(users.get("Bob").unwrap().age, 35);
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! // Iterate over users:
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! for user in &users {
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!     println!("User {}: {}", user.name, user.age);
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! }
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! # }
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! ```
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! Keys don't have to be borrowed from the value. For smaller `Copy` types,
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! it's recommended that you use owned keys. Here's an example of using
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! [`IdOrdMap`] with a small integer key:
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! ```
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! # #[cfg(feature = "std")] {
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! # use iddqd::{IdOrdMap, IdOrdItem, id_upcast};
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! struct Record {
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//!     id: u32,
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!     data: String,
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! }
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//!
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! impl IdOrdItem for Record {
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//!     // The key type is small, so an owned key is preferred.
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!     type Key<'a> = u32;
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!     fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!         self.id
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!     }
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!     id_upcast!();
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! }
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! // ...
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! # }
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! ```
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! An example for [`IdHashMap`], showing a complex borrowed key. Here,
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! "complex" means that the key is not a reference itself, but a struct that
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! returns references to more than one field from the value.
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! ```
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! # #[cfg(feature = "default-hasher")] {
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! use iddqd::{IdHashItem, id_hash_map, id_upcast};
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! #[derive(Debug)]
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! struct Artifact {
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!     name: String,
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!     version: String,
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!     data: Vec<u8>,
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! }
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! // The key type is a borrowed form of the name and version. It needs to
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! // implement `Eq + Hash`.
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! #[derive(Eq, Hash, PartialEq)]
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! struct ArtifactKey<'a> {
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!     name: &'a str,
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!     version: &'a str,
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! }
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! impl IdHashItem for Artifact {
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!     // The key type can borrow from the value.
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//!     type Key<'a> = ArtifactKey<'a>;
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!     fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//!         ArtifactKey { name: &self.name, version: &self.version }
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!     }
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//!
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!     id_upcast!();
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! }
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! // Create a new `IdHashMap` with the given artifacts. This uses the
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! // `id_hash_map!` macro that comes with iddqd.
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! let artifacts = id_hash_map! {
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!     Artifact {
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!         name: "artifact1".to_owned(),
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!         version: "1.0".to_owned(),
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!         data: b"data1".to_vec(),
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//!     },
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!     Artifact {
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!         name: "artifact2".to_owned(),
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//!         version: "1.0".to_owned(),
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!         data: b"data2".to_vec(),
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//!     },
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! };
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//!
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! // Look up artifacts by name and version.
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! assert_eq!(
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//!     artifacts
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//!         .get(&ArtifactKey { name: "artifact1", version: "1.0" })
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//!         .unwrap()
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//!         .data,
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//!     b"data1",
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//! );
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! # }
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! ```
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//!
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! For more examples, see the
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! [examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd/examples)
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! and [extended
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples)
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! directories.
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! ### `Equivalent` and `Comparable`
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! An important feature of the standard library's maps is that they allow any
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! borrowed form of the key type to be used for lookups; for example, a
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! `HashMap<String, T>` type can be looked up with a `&str` key. This is done
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! through the [`Borrow`] trait.
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//!
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! But the [`Borrow`] trait is a bit too restrictive for complex keys such as
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! `ArtifactKey` above, requiring workarounds such as [dynamic
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! dispatch](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example). To
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! address this, the crates.io ecosystem has standardized on the [`Equivalent`]
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! and [`Comparable`] traits as generalizations of `Borrow`. The map types in
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! this crate require these traits.
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! For a key type `T::Key<'_>` and a query type `Q`:
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//!
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! * The hash map types require `Q: Hash + Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. Also, `Q`
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//!   must hash in the same way as `T::Key<'_>`. Typically, this is done by
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//!   ensuring that enum variants and struct fields are in the same
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//!   order[^proptest].
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! * [`IdOrdMap`] requires `Q: Comparable<T::Key<'_>>`, which in turn requires
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//!   `Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. (There's no need for `Q` to implement `Ord` or
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//!   `Eq` itself.)
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//!
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! [^proptest]: We recommend that you test this with e.g. a property-based
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!   test: see [this
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//!   example](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example/blob/a6f17699/src/lib.rs#L233).
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//!
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! Continuing the `ArtifactKey` example from above, we can perform a lookup
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! using a key of this owned form:
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//!
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! ```
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! # #[cfg(feature = "default-hasher")] {
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! use equivalent::Equivalent;
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! # use iddqd::{id_hash_map, IdHashItem, id_upcast};
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! # #[derive(Debug)]
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! # struct Artifact {
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! #     name: String,
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//! #     version: String,
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! #     data: Vec<u8>,
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! # }
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! # #[derive(Eq, Hash, PartialEq)]
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! # struct ArtifactKey<'a> {
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! #     name: &'a str,
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//! #     version: &'a str,
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//! # }
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//! # impl IdHashItem for Artifact {
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//! #     type Key<'a> = ArtifactKey<'a>;
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! #     fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! #         ArtifactKey {
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//! #             name: &self.name,
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//! #             version: &self.version,
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! #         }
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! #     }
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//! #     id_upcast!();
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//! # }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! # let artifacts = id_hash_map! {
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! #     Artifact {
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//! #         name: "artifact1".to_owned(),
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! #         version: "1.0".to_owned(),
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//! #         data: b"data1".to_vec(),
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! #     }
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! # };
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//!
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//! // This is an owned form of ArtifactKey. The fields are in the same
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! // order as ArtifactKey's fields, so it hashes the same way.
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//! #[derive(Hash)]
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//! struct OwnedArtifactKey {
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//!     name: String,
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!     version: String,
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! }
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//!
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! impl Equivalent<ArtifactKey<'_>> for OwnedArtifactKey {
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//!     fn equivalent(&self, other: &ArtifactKey<'_>) -> bool {
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//!         self.name == other.name && self.version == other.version
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//!     }
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//! }
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//!
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//! // Now you can use OwnedArtifactKey to look up the artifact.
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//! let owned_key = OwnedArtifactKey {
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//!     name: "artifact1".to_owned(),
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//!     version: "1.0".to_owned(),
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//! };
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//! assert_eq!(artifacts.get(&owned_key).unwrap().data, b"data1",);
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//! # }
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! ```
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//!
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//! There's a blanket implementation of [`Equivalent`] and [`Comparable`] for
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//! [`Borrow`], so if your type already implements [`Borrow`], there aren't any
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//! extra steps to take.
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//!
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//! # Testing and verification
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//!
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//! This crate is validated through a combination of:
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//!
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//! * Unit tests
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//! * Property-based tests using a naive map as an oracle
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//! * Unit and property-based tests for several kinds of pathological `Eq`,
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//!   `Hash` and `Ord` implementations
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//! * Property-based tests for panic safety
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//! * Miri tests for unsafe code, checked against both Stacked and Tree Borrows
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//! * Compile-fail UI tests to ensure invalid patterns are rejected by the
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//!   borrow checker
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//! * Bounded formal verification for core invariants and UB using
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//!   [Soteria](https://soteria-tools.com)
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//!
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//! Pathological user implementations written in safe Rust might corrupt
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//! internal map state and result in panics, but should never cause UB.
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//!
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//! For more information on our validation philosophy, see [this Oxide blog
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//! entry](https://oxide.computer/blog/iddqd-unsafe).
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//!
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//! If you see a gap in testing, new tests are welcome. Thank you!
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//!
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! Note that **testing requires [cargo-nextest](https://nexte.st/)**: several
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//! tests depend on nextest's process-per-test model.
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//!
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//! # No-std compatibility
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//!
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//! Most of this crate is no-std compatible, though [`alloc`] is required.
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//!
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//! The [`IdOrdMap`] type is not currently no-std compatible due to its use of a
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//! thread-local. This thread-local is just a way to work around a limitation in
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//! std's `BTreeMap` API, though. Either a custom B-Tree implementation, or a
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//! platform-specific notion of thread locals, would suffice to make
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//! [`IdOrdMap`] no-std compatible.
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//!
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//! # Optional features
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//!
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//! - `allocator-api2`: Enables support for custom allocators via the
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//!   [`allocator_api2`] crate. Both global and scoped/arena allocators
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//!   (such as `bumpalo`) are supported. Custom allocators are not currently
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//!   supported by `IdOrdMap`.
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//! - `daft`: Enables [`daft`] support for all ID map types. *Not enabled by
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//!   default.*
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//! - `default-hasher`: Enables the `DefaultHashBuilder` type. Disable this
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//!   feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed into
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//!   [`IdHashMap`], [`BiHashMap`], and [`TriHashMap`]. *Enabled by default.*
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//! - `proptest`: Enables [`proptest`] support for all ID map types, providing
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//!   [`Arbitrary`] implementations and strategies for property-based testing.
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//!   *Not enabled by default.*
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//! - `schemars08`: Enables [`schemars`] support for all ID map types,
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//!   including support for [automatic replacement] through [`typify`] or
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//!   [`dropshot`]. *Not enabled by default.*
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//! - `serde`: Enables serde support for all ID map types. *Not enabled by
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//!   default.*
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//! - `std`: Enables std support. *Enabled by default.*
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//!
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//! # Related work
[338](https://docs.rs#338)//!
[339](https://docs.rs#339)//! - [`bimap`](https://docs.rs/bimap) provides a bijective map, but does not
[340](https://docs.rs#340)//!   have a way to associate arbitrary values with each pair of keys. However,
[341](https://docs.rs#341)//!   it does support an ordered map type without the need for std.
[342](https://docs.rs#342)//!
[343](https://docs.rs#343)//! - [`multi_index_map`](https://crates.io/crates/multi_index_map) provides
[344](https://docs.rs#344)//!   maps with arbitrary indexes on fields, and is more flexible than this
[345](https://docs.rs#345)//!   crate. However, it doesn't expose generic traits for map types, and it
[346](https://docs.rs#346)//!   requires key types to be `Clone`. In `iddqd`, we pick a somewhat different
[347](https://docs.rs#347)//!   point in the design space, but we think `multi_index_map` is also great.
[348](https://docs.rs#348)//!
[349](https://docs.rs#349)//! - In general, this is similar to relational database records with
[350](https://docs.rs#350)//!   indexes. For sufficiently complex use cases, consider an embedded
[351](https://docs.rs#351)//!   database like [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/), or even a networked
[352](https://docs.rs#352)//!   database like [PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/). `iddqd` is a
[353](https://docs.rs#353)//!   good fit for simple in-memory caches of data stored in these databases.
[354](https://docs.rs#354)//!
[355](https://docs.rs#355)//! # Minimum supported Rust version (MSRV)
[356](https://docs.rs#356)//!
[357](https://docs.rs#357)//! This crate's MSRV is **Rust 1.85**. In general we aim for 6 months of Rust
[358](https://docs.rs#358)//! compatibility.
[359](https://docs.rs#359)//!
[360](https://docs.rs#360)//! # What does iddqd mean?
[361](https://docs.rs#361)//!
[362](https://docs.rs#362)//! The name `iddqd` is a reference to [a cheat
[363](https://docs.rs#363)//! code](https://doomwiki.org/wiki/Doom_cheat_codes) in the classic video game
[364](https://docs.rs#364)//! _Doom_. It has `id` in the name, and is short and memorable.
[365](https://docs.rs#365)//!

# IdOrdMap in iddqd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.5/iddqd/struct.IdOrdMap.html

`pub struct IdOrdMap<T> { /* private fields */ }`**crate feature**only.

`std`## Expand description

An ordered map where the keys are part of the values, based on a B-Tree.

The storage mechanism is a fast hash table of integer indexes to items, with the indexes stored in a B-Tree map.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
// Define a struct with a key.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct MyItem {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
// Implement IdOrdItem for the struct.
impl IdOrdItem for MyItem {
    // Keys can borrow from the item.
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
// Create an IdOrdMap and insert items.
let mut map = IdOrdMap::new();
map.insert_unique(MyItem { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(MyItem { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 20 }).unwrap();
// Look up items by their keys.
assert_eq!(map.get("foo").unwrap().value, 42);
assert_eq!(map.get("bar").unwrap().value, 20);
assert!(map.get("baz").is_none());
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a new `IdOrdMap` with the given capacity.

The capacity will be used to initialize the underlying hash table.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]

    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdOrdItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let map: IdOrdMap<Item> = IdOrdMap::with_capacity(10);
assert!(map.capacity() >= 10);
assert!(map.is_empty());
```

#### pub fn [from_iter_unique](https://docs.rs#method.from_iter_unique)<I: [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)<Item = T>>(
    iter: I,

Constructs a new `IdOrdMap` from an iterator of values, rejecting
duplicates.

To overwrite duplicates instead, use [ IdOrdMap::from_iter](https://docs.rs/struct.IdOrdMap.html#method.from_iter).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdOrdItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let items = vec![
    Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 },
    Item { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 99 },
];
// Successful creation with unique keys
let map = IdOrdMap::from_iter_unique(items).unwrap();
assert_eq!(map.len(), 2);
assert_eq!(map.get("foo").unwrap().value, 42);
// Error with duplicate keys
let duplicate_items = vec![
    Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 },
    Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 99 },
];
assert!(IdOrdMap::from_iter_unique(duplicate_items).is_err());
```
Returns true if the map is empty.

Reserves capacity for at least `additional` more elements to be inserted
in the `IdOrdMap`. The collection may reserve more space to
speculatively avoid frequent reallocations. After calling `reserve`,
capacity will be greater than or equal to `self.len() + additional`.
Does nothing if capacity is already sufficient.

Note: This only reserves capacity in the item storage. The internal
`BTreeMap` used for key-to-item mapping does not support capacity
reservation.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the new capacity overflows [ isize::MAX](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.isize.html) bytes, and

[s the program in case of an allocation error.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/alloc/fn.handle_alloc_error.html)

`abort`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdOrdItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map: IdOrdMap<Item> = IdOrdMap::new();
map.reserve(100);
assert!(map.capacity() >= 100);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp.rs.html#437-455)#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://docs.rs#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp.rs.html#437-455)

#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://docs.rs#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

Shrinks the capacity of the map as much as possible. It will drop down as much as possible while maintaining the internal rules and possibly leaving some space in accordance with the resize policy.

Note: This only shrinks the item storage capacity. The internal
`BTreeMap` used for key-to-item mapping does not support capacity
control.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-9)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdOrdItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map: IdOrdMap<Item> = IdOrdMap::with_capacity(100);
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 1 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 2 }).unwrap();
assert!(map.capacity() >= 100);
map.shrink_to_fit();
assert!(map.capacity() >= 2);
```
Shrinks the capacity of the map with a lower limit. It will drop down no lower than the supplied limit while maintaining the internal rules and possibly leaving some space in accordance with the resize policy.

If the current capacity is less than the lower limit, this is a no-op.

Note: This only shrinks the item storage capacity. The internal
`BTreeMap` used for key-to-item mapping does not support capacity
control.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdOrdItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map: IdOrdMap<Item> = IdOrdMap::with_capacity(100);
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 1 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 2 }).unwrap();
assert!(map.capacity() >= 100);
map.shrink_to(10);
assert!(map.capacity() >= 10);
map.shrink_to(0);
assert!(map.capacity() >= 2);
```
Iterates over the items in the map.

Similar to [ BTreeMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/collections/btree/map/struct.BTreeMap.html), the iteration is ordered by

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.IdOrdItem.html#associatedtype.Key)

`T::Key`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdOrdItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map = IdOrdMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "charlie".to_string(), value: 30 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "alice".to_string(), value: 42 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "bob".to_string(), value: 99 }).unwrap();
// Iteration is ordered by key
let mut iter = map.iter();
let item = iter.next().unwrap();
assert_eq!(item.id, "alice");
let item = iter.next().unwrap();
assert_eq!(item.id, "bob");
let item = iter.next().unwrap();
assert_eq!(item.id, "charlie");
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```
Iterates over the items in the map, allowing for mutation.

Similar to [ BTreeMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/collections/btree/map/struct.BTreeMap.html), the iteration is ordered by

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.IdOrdItem.html#associatedtype.Key)

    }

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp.rs.html#754-769)#### pub fn [insert_overwrite](https://docs.rs#method.insert_overwrite)(&mut self, value: T) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp.rs.html#754-769)

#### pub fn [insert_overwrite](https://docs.rs#method.insert_overwrite)(&mut self, value: T) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>

Inserts a value into the map, removing and returning the conflicting item, if any.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdOrdItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map = IdOrdMap::new();
// First insertion - no conflict
let old = map.insert_overwrite(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 });
assert!(old.is_none());
// Overwrite existing key - returns old value
let old = map.insert_overwrite(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 99 });
assert!(old.is_some());
assert_eq!(old.unwrap().value, 42);
// Verify new value is in the map
assert_eq!(map.get("foo").unwrap().value, 99);
```

impl IdOrdItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map = IdOrdMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 }).unwrap();
assert!(map.contains_key("foo"));
assert!(!map.contains_key("bar"));
```

Retrieves an entry by its `key`.

Due to borrow checker limitations, this always accepts an owned key rather than a borrowed form.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-19)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_ord_map, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdOrdItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map = IdOrdMap::new();
// Insert via vacant entry
match map.entry("foo") {
    id_ord_map::Entry::Vacant(entry) => {
        entry.insert(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 });
    }
    id_ord_map::Entry::Occupied(_) => {}
}
// Update via occupied entry
match map.entry("foo") {
    id_ord_map::Entry::Occupied(mut entry) => {
        entry.get_mut().value = 99;
    }
    id_ord_map::Entry::Vacant(_) => {}
}
assert_eq!(map.get("foo").unwrap().value, 99);
```

Retains only the elements specified by the predicate.

In other words, remove all items `T` for which `f(RefMut<T>)` returns
false. The elements are visited in ascending key order.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-26)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdOrdItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map = IdOrdMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 20 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "baz".to_string(), value: 99 }).unwrap();
// Retain only items where value is greater than 30
map.retain(|item| item.value > 30);
assert_eq!(map.len(), 2);
assert_eq!(map.get("foo").unwrap().value, 42);
assert_eq!(map.get("baz").unwrap().value, 99);
assert!(map.get("bar").is_none());
```

The `FromIterator` implementation for `IdOrdMap` overwrites duplicate
items.

To reject duplicates, use [ IdOrdMap::from_iter_unique](https://docs.rs/struct.IdOrdMap.html#method.from_iter_unique).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-27)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdOrdItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let items = vec![
    Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 },
    Item { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 20 },
    Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 100 }, // duplicate key, overwrites
];
let map: IdOrdMap<Item> = items.into_iter().collect();
assert_eq!(map.len(), 2);
assert_eq!(map.get("foo").unwrap().value, 100); // last value wins
assert_eq!(map.get("bar").unwrap().value, 20);
```

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-IdOrdMap%3CT%3E)

**crate feature**only.

`serde`An `IdOrdMap` serializes to the list of items. Items are serialized in
order of their keys.

Serializing as a list of items rather than as a map works around the lack of non-string keys in formats like JSON.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-28)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Debug, Serialize)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    email: String,
}
// This is a complex key, so it can't be a JSON map key.
#[derive(Eq, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct ComplexKey<'a> {
    id: u32,
    email: &'a str,
}
impl IdOrdItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = ComplexKey<'a>;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        ComplexKey { id: self.id, email: &self.email }
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map = IdOrdMap::<Item>::new();
map.insert_unique(Item {
    id: 1,
    name: "Alice".to_string(),
    email: "alice@example.com".to_string(),
})
.unwrap();
// The map is serialized as a list of items in order of their keys.
let serialized = serde_json::to_string(&map).unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    serialized,
    r#"[{"id":1,"name":"Alice","email":"alice@example.com"}]"#,
);
```

# IdHashMap in iddqd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.5/iddqd/struct.IdHashMap.html

`pub struct IdHashMap<T, S = `[DefaultHashBuilder](https://docs.rs/type.DefaultHashBuilder.html), A: [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html) = [Global](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/global/struct.Global.html)> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

A hash map where the key is part of the value.

The storage mechanism is a fast hash table of integer indexes to items, with these indexes stored in a hash table. This allows for efficient lookups by the key and prevents duplicates.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, IdHashMap, id_upcast};
// Define a struct with a key.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct MyItem {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
// Implement IdHashItem for the struct.
impl IdHashItem for MyItem {
    // Keys can borrow from the item.
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
// Create an IdHashMap and insert items.
let mut map = IdHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(MyItem { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(MyItem { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 20 }).unwrap();
// Look up items by their keys.
assert_eq!(map.get("foo").unwrap().value, 42);
assert_eq!(map.get("bar").unwrap().value, 20);
assert!(map.get("baz").is_none());
```

Clears the map, removing all items.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```

Reserves capacity for at least `additional` more elements to be inserted
in the `IdHashMap`. The collection may reserve more space to
speculatively avoid frequent reallocations. After calling `reserve`,
capacity will be greater than or equal to `self.len() + additional`.
Does nothing if capacity is already sufficient.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the new capacity overflows [ isize::MAX](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.isize.html) bytes, and

[s the program in case of an allocation error. Use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/alloc/fn.handle_alloc_error.html)

`abort`[instead if you want to handle memory allocation failure.](https://docs.rs/struct.IdHashMap.html#method.try_reserve)

`try_reserve`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, IdHashMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdHashItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map: IdHashMap<Item> = IdHashMap::new();
map.reserve(100);
assert!(map.capacity() >= 100);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp.rs.html#693-703)#### pub fn [try_reserve](https://docs.rs#method.try_reserve)(&mut self, additional: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [TryReserveError](https://docs.rs/errors/struct.TryReserveError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp.rs.html#693-703)

#### pub fn [try_reserve](https://docs.rs#method.try_reserve)(&mut self, additional: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [TryReserveError](https://docs.rs/errors/struct.TryReserveError.html)>

Tries to reserve capacity for at least `additional` more elements to be
inserted in the `IdHashMap`. The collection may reserve more space to
speculatively avoid frequent reallocations. After calling `try_reserve`,
capacity will be greater than or equal to `self.len() + additional` if
it returns `Ok(())`. Does nothing if capacity is already sufficient.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the capacity overflows, or the allocator reports a failure, then an error is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

If reservation fails partway through, some internal structures may have already increased their capacity. The map remains in a valid state but may have uneven capacities across its internal structures.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, IdHashMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdHashItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map: IdHashMap<Item> = IdHashMap::new();
map.try_reserve(100).expect("allocation should succeed");
assert!(map.capacity() >= 100);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp.rs.html#737-754)#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://docs.rs#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp.rs.html#737-754)

#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://docs.rs#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

Shrinks the capacity of the map as much as possible. It will drop down as much as possible while maintaining the internal rules and possibly leaving some space in accordance with the resize policy.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, IdHashMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdHashItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map: IdHashMap<Item> = IdHashMap::with_capacity(100);
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 1 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 2 }).unwrap();
assert!(map.capacity() >= 100);
map.shrink_to_fit();
assert!(map.capacity() >= 2);
```
Shrinks the capacity of the map with a lower limit. It will drop down no lower than the supplied limit while maintaining the internal rules and possibly leaving some space in accordance with the resize policy.

If the current capacity is less than the lower limit, this is a no-op.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-17)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, IdHashMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdHashItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map: IdHashMap<Item> = IdHashMap::with_capacity(100);
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 1 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 2 }).unwrap();
assert!(map.capacity() >= 100);
map.shrink_to(10);
assert!(map.capacity() >= 10);
map.shrink_to(0);
assert!(map.capacity() >= 2);
```
Iterates over the items in the map.

Similar to [ HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html), the iteration order is arbitrary and not
guaranteed to be stable.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-18)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, IdHashMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdHashItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map = IdHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 20 }).unwrap();
let mut values: Vec<u32> = map.iter().map(|item| item.value).collect();
values.sort();
assert_eq!(values, vec![20, 42]);
```
Iterates over the items in the map, allowing for mutation.

Similar to [ HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html), the iteration order is arbitrary and not
guaranteed to be stable.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-19)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, IdHashMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdHashItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map = IdHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 20 }).unwrap();
for mut item in map.iter_mut() {
    item.value *= 2;
}
assert_eq!(map.get("foo").unwrap().value, 84);
assert_eq!(map.get("bar").unwrap().value, 40);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp.rs.html#981-996)

#### pub fn [insert_overwrite](https://docs.rs#method.insert_overwrite)(&mut self, value: T) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>

Inserts a value into the map, removing and returning the conflicting item, if any.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-20)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, IdHashMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdHashItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map = IdHashMap::new();
// First insertion returns None
let old = map.insert_overwrite(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 });
assert!(old.is_none());
// Second insertion with same key returns the old value
let old = map.insert_overwrite(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 100 });
assert_eq!(old.unwrap().value, 42);
assert_eq!(map.get("foo").unwrap().value, 100);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp.rs.html#1039-1045)#### pub fn [insert_unique](https://docs.rs#method.insert_unique)(&mut self, value: T) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [DuplicateItem](https://docs.rs/errors/struct.DuplicateItem.html)<T, [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp.rs.html#1039-1045)

#### pub fn [insert_unique](https://docs.rs#method.insert_unique)(&mut self, value: T) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [DuplicateItem](https://docs.rs/errors/struct.DuplicateItem.html)<T, [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)>>

Inserts a value into the set, returning an error if any duplicates were added.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-21)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, IdHashMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdHashItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map = IdHashMap::new();
// First insertion succeeds
assert!(
    map.insert_unique(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 }).is_ok()
);
// Second insertion with different key succeeds
assert!(
    map.insert_unique(Item { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 20 }).is_ok()
);
// Third insertion with duplicate key fails
assert!(
    map.insert_unique(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 100 }).is_err()
);
```

Gets a mutable reference to the value associated with the given key.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-24)Examples

```

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]

    value: u32,

Removes an item from the map by its key.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-25)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, IdHashMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]

        &self.id
    }

Retrieves an entry by its key.

Due to borrow checker limitations, this always accepts an owned key rather than a borrowed form of it.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-26)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, IdHashMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdHashItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map = IdHashMap::new();
// Use entry API for conditional insertion
map.entry("foo").or_insert(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 });
map.entry("bar").or_insert(Item { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 20 });
assert_eq!(map.len(), 2);
```
Retains only the elements specified by the predicate.

In other words, remove all items `T` for which `f(RefMut<T>)` returns
false. The elements are visited in an arbitrary order.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-27)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, IdHashMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdHashItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map = IdHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 20 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "baz".to_string(), value: 99 }).unwrap();
// Retain only items where value is greater than 30
map.retain(|item| item.value > 30);
assert_eq!(map.len(), 2);
assert_eq!(map.get("foo").unwrap().value, 42);
assert_eq!(map.get("baz").unwrap().value, 99);
assert!(map.get("bar").is_none());
```

### impl<'de, T, S: [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html) + [Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html), A: [Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) + [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html)> [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)<'de> for [IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdHashMap.html)<T, S, A>

**crate feature**only.

`serde`The `Deserialize` impl for `IdHashMap` deserializes from either a sequence
or a map of items, then rebuilds the indexes and produces an error if there
are any duplicates.

In case a map is deserialized, the key is not deserialized or verified against the value. (In general, verification is not possible because the key type has a lifetime parameter embedded in it.)

The `fmt::Debug` bound on `T` ensures better error reporting.
