### impl<T: [IdHashItem](https://docs.rs/trait.IdHashItem.html), S: [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html), A: [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html)> [Extend](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.Extend.html)<T> for [IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdHashMap.html)<T, S, A>

The `Extend` implementation overwrites duplicates. In the future, there will
also be an `extend_unique` method that will return an error.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-28)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, IdHashMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdHashItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map = IdHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 }).unwrap();
let new_items = vec![
    Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 100 }, // overwrites existing
    Item { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 20 },  // new item
];
map.extend(new_items);
assert_eq!(map.len(), 2);
assert_eq!(map.get("foo").unwrap().value, 100); // overwritten
assert_eq!(map.get("bar").unwrap().value, 20); // new
```

### impl<T: [IdHashItem](https://docs.rs/trait.IdHashItem.html), S: [Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) + [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html), A: [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html) + [Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html)> [FromIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.FromIterator.html)<T> for [IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdHashMap.html)<T, S, A>

The `FromIterator` implementation for `IdHashMap` overwrites duplicate
items.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-29)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, IdHashMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl IdHashItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let items = vec![
    Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 },
    Item { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 20 },
    Item { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 100 }, // duplicate key, overwrites
];
let map: IdHashMap<Item> = items.into_iter().collect();
assert_eq!(map.len(), 2);
assert_eq!(map.get("foo").unwrap().value, 100); // last value wins
assert_eq!(map.get("bar").unwrap().value, 20);
```

### impl<'a, T: [IdHashItem](https://docs.rs/trait.IdHashItem.html), S: [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html), A: [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html)> [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html) for &'a [IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdHashMap.html)<T, S, A>

### impl<T, S: [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html), A: [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html)> [Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html) for [IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdHashMap.html)<T, S, A>

**crate feature**only.

`serde`An `IdHashMap` serializes to the list of items. Items are serialized in
arbitrary order.

Serializing as a list of items rather than as a map works around the lack of non-string keys in formats like JSON.

To serialize as a map instead, see [ IdHashMapAsMap](https://docs.rs/id_hash_map/struct.IdHashMapAsMap.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-33)Examples

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, IdHashMap, id_upcast};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Debug, Serialize)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    email: String,
}
// This is a complex key, so it can't be a JSON map key.
#[derive(Eq, Hash, PartialEq)]
struct ComplexKey<'a> {
    id: u32,
    email: &'a str,
}
impl IdHashItem for Item {
    type Key<'a> = ComplexKey<'a>;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        ComplexKey { id: self.id, email: &self.email }
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut map = IdHashMap::<Item>::new();
map.insert_unique(Item {
    id: 1,
    name: "Alice".to_string(),
    email: "alice@example.com".to_string(),
})
.unwrap();
// The map is serialized as a list of items.
let serialized = serde_json::to_string(&map).unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    serialized,
    r#"[{"id":1,"name":"Alice","email":"alice@example.com"}]"#,
);
```

# BiHashMap in iddqd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.5/iddqd/struct.BiHashMap.html

`pub struct BiHashMap<T, S = `[DefaultHashBuilder](https://docs.rs/type.DefaultHashBuilder.html), A: [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html) = [Global](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/global/struct.Global.html)> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

A 1:1 (bijective) map for two keys and a value.

The storage mechanism is a fast hash table of integer indexes to items, with these indexes stored in two hash tables. This allows for efficient lookups by either of the two keys and prevents duplicates.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use iddqd::{BiHashItem, BiHashMap, bi_upcast};
// Define a struct with two keys and a value.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct MyItem {
    id: u32,
    name: &'static str,
    value: i32,
}
// Implement BiHashItem for the struct.
impl BiHashItem for MyItem {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
// Create a new BiHashMap and insert items.
let mut map = BiHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(MyItem { id: 1, name: "foo", value: 42 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(MyItem { id: 2, name: "bar", value: 99 }).unwrap();
// Look up by the first key.
assert_eq!(map.get1(&1).unwrap().value, 42);
assert_eq!(map.get1(&2).unwrap().value, 99);
assert!(map.get1(&3).is_none());
// Look up by the second key.
assert_eq!(map.get2(&"foo").unwrap().value, 42);
assert_eq!(map.get2(&"bar").unwrap().value, 99);
assert!(map.get2(&"baz").is_none());
```

Reserves capacity for at least `additional` more elements to be inserted
in the `BiHashMap`. The collection may reserve more space to
speculatively avoid frequent reallocations. After calling `reserve`,
capacity will be greater than or equal to `self.len() + additional`.
Does nothing if capacity is already sufficient.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the new capacity overflows [ isize::MAX](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.isize.html) bytes, and

[s the program in case of an allocation error. Use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/alloc/fn.handle_alloc_error.html)

`abort`[instead if you want to handle memory allocation failure.](https://docs.rs/struct.BiHashMap.html#method.try_reserve)

`try_reserve`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```

    id: u32,
    name: String,

    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
let mut map: BiHashMap<Item> = BiHashMap::new();
map.reserve(100);
assert!(map.capacity() >= 100);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/bi_hash_map/imp.rs.html#867-881)#### pub fn [try_reserve](https://docs.rs#method.try_reserve)(&mut self, additional: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [TryReserveError](https://docs.rs/errors/struct.TryReserveError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/bi_hash_map/imp.rs.html#867-881)

#### pub fn [try_reserve](https://docs.rs#method.try_reserve)(&mut self, additional: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [TryReserveError](https://docs.rs/errors/struct.TryReserveError.html)>

Tries to reserve capacity for at least `additional` more elements to be
inserted in the `BiHashMap`. The collection may reserve more space to
speculatively avoid frequent reallocations. After calling `try_reserve`,
capacity will be greater than or equal to `self.len() + additional` if
it returns `Ok(())`. Does nothing if capacity is already sufficient.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the capacity overflows, or the allocator reports a failure, then an error is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

If reservation fails partway through, some internal structures may have already increased their capacity. The map remains in a valid state but may have uneven capacities across its internal structures.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

```
use iddqd::{BiHashItem, BiHashMap, bi_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
}
impl BiHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
let mut map: BiHashMap<Item> = BiHashMap::new();
map.try_reserve(100).expect("allocation should succeed");
assert!(map.capacity() >= 100);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/bi_hash_map/imp.rs.html#919-938)#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://docs.rs#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/bi_hash_map/imp.rs.html#919-938)

#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://docs.rs#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

Shrinks the capacity of the map as much as possible. It will drop down as much as possible while maintaining the internal rules and possibly leaving some space in accordance with the resize policy.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

```
use iddqd::{BiHashItem, BiHashMap, bi_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
}
impl BiHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
let mut map: BiHashMap<Item> = BiHashMap::with_capacity(100);
map.insert_unique(Item { id: 1, name: "foo".to_string() }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: 2, name: "bar".to_string() }).unwrap();
assert!(map.capacity() >= 100);
map.shrink_to_fit();
assert!(map.capacity() >= 2);
```
Shrinks the capacity of the map with a lower limit. It will drop down no lower than the supplied limit while maintaining the internal rules and possibly leaving some space in accordance with the resize policy.

If the current capacity is less than the lower limit, this is a no-op.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-17)Examples

```
use iddqd::{BiHashItem, BiHashMap, bi_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
}
impl BiHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
let mut map: BiHashMap<Item> = BiHashMap::with_capacity(100);
map.insert_unique(Item { id: 1, name: "foo".to_string() }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: 2, name: "bar".to_string() }).unwrap();
assert!(map.capacity() >= 100);
map.shrink_to(10);
assert!(map.capacity() >= 10);
map.shrink_to(0);
assert!(map.capacity() >= 2);
```
Returns an iterator over all items in the map.

Similar to [ HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html), the iteration order is arbitrary and not
guaranteed to be stable.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-18)Examples

```
use iddqd::{BiHashItem, BiHashMap, bi_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    value: i32,
}
impl BiHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
let mut map = BiHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: 1, name: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 })
    .unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: 2, name: "bar".to_string(), value: 99 })
    .unwrap();
let mut values: Vec<i32> = map.iter().map(|item| item.value).collect();
values.sort();
assert_eq!(values, vec![42, 99]);
```
Iterates over the items in the map, allowing for mutation.

Similar to [ HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html), the iteration order is arbitrary and not
guaranteed to be stable.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-19)Examples

```

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    value: i32,
}
impl BiHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
let mut map = BiHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: 1, name: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 })
    .unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: 2, name: "bar".to_string(), value: 99 })
    .unwrap();
for mut item in map.iter_mut() {
    item.value += 10;
}
assert_eq!(map.get1(&1).unwrap().value, 52);
assert_eq!(map.get1(&2).unwrap().value, 109);
```

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-20)Examples

```
use iddqd::{BiHashItem, BiHashMap, bi_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    value: i32,
}
impl BiHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}

map.insert_unique(Item { id: 1, name: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 })
    .unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: 2, name: "bar".to_string(), value: 99 })
    .unwrap();
// Insert an item with conflicting key1
let removed = map.insert_overwrite(Item {
    id: 1,
    name: "baz".to_string(),

assert_eq!(removed[0].name, "foo");
assert_eq!(removed[0].value, 42);

#### pub fn [contains_key_unique](https://docs.rs#method.contains_key_unique)<'a, Q1, Q2>(&'a self, key1: [&Q1](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html), key2: [&Q2](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns true if the map contains a single item that matches both `key1` and `key2`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-22)Examples

```
use iddqd::{BiHashItem, BiHashMap, bi_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    value: i32,
}
impl BiHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
let mut map = BiHashMap::new();

map.insert_unique(Item { id: 2, name: "bar".to_string(), value: 99 }).unwrap();

assert!(map.contains_key_unique(&2, &"bar"));
assert!(!map.contains_key_unique(&1, &"bar")); // key1 exists but key2 doesn't match

Retrieves an entry by its keys.

Due to borrow checker limitations, this always accepts owned keys rather than a borrowed form of them.

[§](https://docs.rs#differences-from-single-key-entries)Differences from single-key entries

The [ Entry](https://docs.rs/bi_hash_map/enum.Entry.html) returned by this method differs from those provided
for the other map types, because it is possible for one of the two keys
provided to correspond to an existing entry, while the other does not.

For more information, and examples covering non-unique entries, see the
type-level documentation for [ Entry](https://docs.rs/bi_hash_map/enum.Entry.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-31)Examples

```
use iddqd::{BiHashItem, BiHashMap, bi_hash_map, bi_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    value: i32,
}
impl BiHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
let mut map = BiHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: 1, name: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 })
    .unwrap();
// Get an existing entry.
match map.entry(1, "foo") {
    bi_hash_map::Entry::Occupied(entry) => {
        assert_eq!(entry.get().as_unique().unwrap().value, 42);
    }
    bi_hash_map::Entry::Vacant(_) => panic!("Should be occupied"),
}
// Try to get a non-existing entry.
match map.entry(2, "bar") {
    bi_hash_map::Entry::Occupied(_) => panic!("Should be vacant"),
    bi_hash_map::Entry::Vacant(entry) => {
        entry.insert(Item { id: 2, name: "bar".to_string(), value: 99 });
    }
}
assert_eq!(map.len(), 2);
```
For an expanded example, see the type-level documentation for [ Entry](https://docs.rs/bi_hash_map/enum.Entry.html).

Retains only the elements specified by the predicate.

In other words, remove all items `T` for which `f(RefMut<T>)` returns
false. The elements are visited in an arbitrary order.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-32)Examples

```
use iddqd::{BiHashItem, BiHashMap, bi_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl BiHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
let mut map = BiHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: 1, name: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 })
    .unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: 2, name: "bar".to_string(), value: 20 })
    .unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: 3, name: "baz".to_string(), value: 99 })
    .unwrap();
// Retain only items where value is greater than 30
map.retain(|item| item.value > 30);
assert_eq!(map.len(), 2);
assert_eq!(map.get1(&1).unwrap().value, 42);
assert_eq!(map.get1(&3).unwrap().value, 99);
assert!(map.get1(&2).is_none());
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/bi_hash_map/serde_impls.rs.html#116-168)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-BiHashMap%3CT,+S,+A%3E-2)### impl<'de, T: [BiHashItem](https://docs.rs/trait.BiHashItem.html) + [Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) + [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)<'de>, S: [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html), A: [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html)> [BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.BiHashMap.html)<T, S, A>

### impl<'de, T, S: [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html) + [Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html), A: [Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) + [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html) + [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html)> [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)<'de> for [BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.BiHashMap.html)<T, S, A>

**crate feature**only.

`serde`The `Deserialize` impl for `BiHashMap` deserializes from either a sequence
or a map of items, rebuilding the indexes and producing an error if there
are any duplicates.

In case a map is deserialized, the key is not deserialized or verified against the value. (In general, verification is not possible because the key type has a lifetime parameter embedded in it.)

The `fmt::Debug` bound on `T` ensures better error reporting.

### impl<T: [BiHashItem](https://docs.rs/trait.BiHashItem.html), S: [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html), A: [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html)> [Extend](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.Extend.html)<T> for [BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.BiHashMap.html)<T, S, A>

The `Extend` implementation overwrites duplicates. In the future, there will
also be an `extend_unique` method that will return an error.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-33)Examples

```
use iddqd::{BiHashItem, BiHashMap, bi_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    value: i32,
}
impl BiHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
let mut map = BiHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Item { id: 1, name: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 }).unwrap();
let new_items = vec![
    Item { id: 2, name: "bar".to_string(), value: 99 },
    Item { id: 1, name: "baz".to_string(), value: 100 }, // overwrites existing
];
map.extend(new_items);
assert_eq!(map.len(), 2);
assert_eq!(map.get1(&1).unwrap().name, "baz"); // overwritten
assert_eq!(map.get1(&1).unwrap().value, 100);
```

### impl<T: [BiHashItem](https://docs.rs/trait.BiHashItem.html), S: [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html) + [Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html), A: [Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) + [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html)> [FromIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.FromIterator.html)<T> for [BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.BiHashMap.html)<T, S, A>

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-34)Examples

```
use iddqd::{BiHashItem, BiHashMap, bi_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    value: i32,
}
impl BiHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
let items = vec![
    Item { id: 1, name: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 },
    Item { id: 2, name: "bar".to_string(), value: 99 },
    Item { id: 1, name: "baz".to_string(), value: 100 }, // overwrites first item
];
let map: BiHashMap<Item> = items.into_iter().collect();
assert_eq!(map.len(), 2);
assert_eq!(map.get1(&1).unwrap().name, "baz"); // overwritten
assert_eq!(map.get1(&1).unwrap().value, 100);
assert_eq!(map.get1(&2).unwrap().value, 99);
```

### impl<T: [BiHashItem](https://docs.rs/trait.BiHashItem.html) + [PartialEq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialEq.html), S: [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html), A: [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html)> [PartialEq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialEq.html) for [BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.BiHashMap.html)<T, S, A>

The `PartialEq` implementation for `BiHashMap` checks that both maps have
the same items, regardless of insertion order.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-35)Examples

```
use iddqd::{BiHashItem, BiHashMap, bi_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    value: i32,
}
impl BiHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
let mut map1 = BiHashMap::new();
map1.insert_unique(Item { id: 1, name: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 })
    .unwrap();
map1.insert_unique(Item { id: 2, name: "bar".to_string(), value: 99 })
    .unwrap();
let mut map2 = BiHashMap::new();
map2.insert_unique(Item { id: 2, name: "bar".to_string(), value: 99 })
    .unwrap();
map2.insert_unique(Item { id: 1, name: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 })
    .unwrap();
// Maps are equal even if items were inserted in different order
assert_eq!(map1, map2);
map2.insert_unique(Item { id: 3, name: "baz".to_string(), value: 200 })
    .unwrap();
assert_ne!(map1, map2);
```

### impl<T, S: [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html), A: [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html)> [Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html) for [BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.BiHashMap.html)<T, S, A>

**crate feature**only.

`serde`A `BiHashMap` serializes to the list of items. Items are serialized in
arbitrary order.

Serializing as a list of items rather than as a map works around the lack of non-string keys in formats like JSON.

To serialize as a map instead, see [ BiHashMapAsMap](https://docs.rs/bi_hash_map/struct.BiHashMapAsMap.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-36)Examples

```
use iddqd::{BiHashItem, BiHashMap, bi_upcast};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Debug, Serialize)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    email: String,
    value: usize,
}
// This is a complex key, so it can't be a JSON map key.
#[derive(Eq, Hash, PartialEq)]
struct ComplexKey<'a> {
    name: &'a str,
    email: &'a str,
}
impl BiHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = ComplexKey<'a>;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        ComplexKey { name: &self.name, email: &self.email }
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
let mut map = BiHashMap::<Item>::new();
map.insert_unique(Item {
    id: 1,
    name: "Alice".to_string(),
    email: "alice@example.com".to_string(),
    value: 42,
})
.unwrap();
// The map is serialized as a list of items.
let serialized = serde_json::to_string(&map).unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    serialized,
    r#"[{"id":1,"name":"Alice","email":"alice@example.com","value":42}]"#,
);
```

# TriHashMap in iddqd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.5/iddqd/struct.TriHashMap.html

`pub struct TriHashMap<T, S = `[DefaultHashBuilder](https://docs.rs/type.DefaultHashBuilder.html), A: [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html) = [Global](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/global/struct.Global.html)> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

A 1:1:1 (trijective) map for three keys and a value.

The storage mechanism is a fast hash table of integer indexes to items, with these indexes stored in three hashmaps. This allows for efficient lookups by any of the three keys, while preventing duplicates.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Person {
    id: u32,
    email: String,
    phone: String,
    name: String,
}
// Implement TriHashItem to define the three key types.
impl TriHashItem for Person {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.phone
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
// Create a TriHashMap and insert items.
let mut people = TriHashMap::new();
people
    .insert_unique(Person {
        id: 1,
        email: "alice@example.com".to_string(),
        phone: "555-1234".to_string(),
        name: "Alice".to_string(),
    })
    .unwrap();
// Lookup by any of the three keys.
let person = people.get1(&1).unwrap();
assert_eq!(person.name, "Alice");
let person = people.get2("alice@example.com").unwrap();
assert_eq!(person.id, 1);
let person = people.get3("555-1234").unwrap();
assert_eq!(person.email, "alice@example.com");
```

#### pub fn [with_capacity_and_hasher_in](https://docs.rs#method.with_capacity_and_hasher_in)(capacity: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), hasher: S, alloc: A) -> Self

Creates a new `TriHashMap` with the given capacity, hasher, and
allocator.

Requires the `allocator-api2` feature to be enabled.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

Using the [ bumpalo](https://docs.rs/bumpalo) allocator:

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
use std::collections::hash_map::RandomState;
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Person {
    id: u32,
    email: String,
    phone: String,
    name: String,
}
impl TriHashItem for Person {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.phone
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
// Define a new allocator.
let bump = bumpalo::Bump::new();
let hasher = RandomState::new();
// Create a new TriHashMap with capacity and hasher using the allocator.
let map: TriHashMap<Person, _, &bumpalo::Bump> =
    TriHashMap::with_capacity_and_hasher_in(10, hasher, &bump);
assert!(map.capacity() >= 10);
assert!(map.is_empty());
```

Reserves capacity for at least `additional` more elements to be inserted
in the `TriHashMap`. The collection may reserve more space to
speculatively avoid frequent reallocations. After calling `reserve`,
capacity will be greater than or equal to `self.len() + additional`.
Does nothing if capacity is already sufficient.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the new capacity overflows [ isize::MAX](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.isize.html) bytes, and

[s the program in case of an allocation error. Use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/alloc/fn.handle_alloc_error.html)

`abort`[instead if you want to handle memory allocation failure.](https://docs.rs/struct.TriHashMap.html#method.try_reserve)

`try_reserve`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```

        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let mut map: TriHashMap<Item> = TriHashMap::new();
map.reserve(100);
assert!(map.capacity() >= 100);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp.rs.html#965-983)#### pub fn [try_reserve](https://docs.rs#method.try_reserve)(&mut self, additional: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [TryReserveError](https://docs.rs/errors/struct.TryReserveError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp.rs.html#965-983)

#### pub fn [try_reserve](https://docs.rs#method.try_reserve)(&mut self, additional: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [TryReserveError](https://docs.rs/errors/struct.TryReserveError.html)>

Tries to reserve capacity for at least `additional` more elements to be
inserted in the `TriHashMap`. The collection may reserve more space to
speculatively avoid frequent reallocations. After calling `try_reserve`,
capacity will be greater than or equal to `self.len() + additional` if
it returns `Ok(())`. Does nothing if capacity is already sufficient.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the capacity overflows, or the allocator reports a failure, then an error is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

If reservation fails partway through, some internal structures may have already increased their capacity. The map remains in a valid state but may have uneven capacities across its internal structures.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    email: String,
}
impl TriHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let mut map: TriHashMap<Item> = TriHashMap::new();
map.try_reserve(100).expect("allocation should succeed");
assert!(map.capacity() >= 100);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp.rs.html#1036-1057)#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://docs.rs#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp.rs.html#1036-1057)

#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://docs.rs#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

Shrinks the capacity of the map as much as possible. It will drop down as much as possible while maintaining the internal rules and possibly leaving some space in accordance with the resize policy.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    email: String,
}
impl TriHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let mut map: TriHashMap<Item> = TriHashMap::with_capacity(100);
map.insert_unique(Item {
    id: 1,
    name: "foo".to_string(),
    email: "foo@example.com".to_string(),
})
.unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item {
    id: 2,
    name: "bar".to_string(),
    email: "bar@example.com".to_string(),
})
.unwrap();
assert!(map.capacity() >= 100);
map.shrink_to_fit();
assert!(map.capacity() >= 2);
```
Shrinks the capacity of the map with a lower limit. It will drop down no lower than the supplied limit while maintaining the internal rules and possibly leaving some space in accordance with the resize policy.

If the current capacity is less than the lower limit, this is a no-op.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-17)Examples

```

        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let mut map: TriHashMap<Item> = TriHashMap::with_capacity(100);
map.insert_unique(Item {
    id: 1,
    name: "foo".to_string(),
    email: "foo@example.com".to_string(),

    id: 2,

```
Iterates over the items in the map.

Similar to [ HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html), the iteration order is arbitrary and not
guaranteed to be stable.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-18)Examples

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Person {
    id: u32,
    email: String,
    phone: String,
    name: String,
}
impl TriHashItem for Person {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.phone
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let mut map = TriHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Person {
    id: 1,
    email: "alice@example.com".to_string(),
    phone: "555-1234".to_string(),
    name: "Alice".to_string(),
})
.unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Person {
    id: 2,
    email: "bob@example.com".to_string(),
    phone: "555-5678".to_string(),
    name: "Bob".to_string(),
})
.unwrap();
let mut count = 0;
for person in map.iter() {
    assert!(person.id == 1 || person.id == 2);
    count += 1;
}
assert_eq!(count, 2);
```
Iterates over the items in the map, allowing for mutation.

Similar to [ HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html), the iteration order is arbitrary and not
guaranteed to be stable.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-19)Examples

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Person {
    id: u32,
    email: String,
    phone: String,
    name: String,
}
impl TriHashItem for Person {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.phone
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let mut map = TriHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Person {
    id: 1,
    email: "alice@example.com".to_string(),
    phone: "555-1234".to_string(),
    name: "Alice".to_string(),
})
.unwrap();
for mut person in map.iter_mut() {
    person.name.push_str(" Updated");
}

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp.rs.html#1383-1396)#### pub fn [insert_overwrite](https://docs.rs#method.insert_overwrite)(&mut self, value: T) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp.rs.html#1383-1396)

#### pub fn [insert_overwrite](https://docs.rs#method.insert_overwrite)(&mut self, value: T) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<T>

Inserts a value into the map, removing any conflicting items and returning a list of those items.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-20)Examples

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Person {
    id: u32,
    email: String,
    phone: String,
    name: String,
}
impl TriHashItem for Person {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.phone
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let mut map = TriHashMap::new();
// First insertion - no conflicts
let overwritten = map.insert_overwrite(Person {
    id: 1,
    email: "alice@example.com".to_string(),
    phone: "555-1234".to_string(),
    name: "Alice".to_string(),
});
assert!(overwritten.is_empty());
// Overwrite with same id - returns the old item
let overwritten = map.insert_overwrite(Person {
    id: 1,
    email: "alice.new@example.com".to_string(),
    phone: "555-9999".to_string(),
    name: "Alice New".to_string(),
});
assert_eq!(overwritten.len(), 1);
assert_eq!(overwritten[0].name, "Alice");
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp.rs.html#1488-1539)

#### pub fn [insert_unique](https://docs.rs#method.insert_unique)(&mut self, value: T) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [DuplicateItem](https://docs.rs/errors/struct.DuplicateItem.html)<T, [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)>>

Inserts a value into the set, returning an error if any duplicates were added.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-21)Examples

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Person {
    id: u32,
    email: String,
    phone: String,
    name: String,
}
impl TriHashItem for Person {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.phone
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let mut map = TriHashMap::new();
// Successful insertion
assert!(
    map.insert_unique(Person {
        id: 1,
        email: "alice@example.com".to_string(),
        phone: "555-1234".to_string(),
        name: "Alice".to_string(),
    })
    .is_ok()
);
assert!(
    map.insert_unique(Person {
        id: 2,
        email: "bob@example.com".to_string(),
        phone: "555-5678".to_string(),
        name: "Bob".to_string(),
    })
    .is_ok()
);
// Duplicate key1
assert!(
    map.insert_unique(Person {
        id: 1,
        email: "charlie@example.com".to_string(),
        phone: "555-9999".to_string(),
        name: "Charlie".to_string(),
    })
    .is_err()
);
// Duplicate key2
assert!(
    map.insert_unique(Person {
        id: 3,
        email: "alice@example.com".to_string(),
        phone: "555-7777".to_string(),
        name: "Alice2".to_string(),
    })
    .is_err()
);
// Duplicate key3
assert!(
    map.insert_unique(Person {
        id: 4,
        email: "dave@example.com".to_string(),
        phone: "555-1234".to_string(),
        name: "Dave".to_string(),
    })
    .is_err()
);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp.rs.html#1595-1607)#### pub fn [contains_key_unique](https://docs.rs#method.contains_key_unique)<'a, Q1, Q2, Q3>(
    &'a self,
    key1: [&Q1](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    key2: [&Q2](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    key3: [&Q3](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp.rs.html#1595-1607)

#### pub fn [contains_key_unique](https://docs.rs#method.contains_key_unique)<'a, Q1, Q2, Q3>(
    &'a self,
    key1: [&Q1](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    key2: [&Q2](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    key3: [&Q3](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns true if the map contains a single item that matches all three keys.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-22)Examples

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Person {
    id: u32,
    email: String,
    phone: String,
    name: String,
}
impl TriHashItem for Person {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.phone
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let mut map = TriHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Person {
    id: 1,
    email: "alice@example.com".to_string(),
    phone: "555-1234".to_string(),
    name: "Alice".to_string(),
}).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Person {
    id: 2,
    email: "bob@example.com".to_string(),
    phone: "555-5678".to_string(),
    name: "Bob".to_string(),
}).unwrap();
assert!(map.contains_key_unique(&1, &"alice@example.com", &"555-1234"));
assert!(map.contains_key_unique(&2, &"bob@example.com", &"555-5678"));
assert!(!map.contains_key_unique(&1, &"bob@example.com", &"555-1234")); // key1 exists but key2 doesn't match
assert!(!map.contains_key_unique(&3, &"charlie@example.com", &"555-9999")); // none of the keys exist
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp.rs.html#1663-1681)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp.rs.html#1663-1681)

Gets a reference to the unique item associated with the given `key1`,
`key2`, and `key3`, if it exists.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-23)Examples

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Person {
    id: u32,
    email: String,
    phone: String,
    name: String,
}
impl TriHashItem for Person {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.phone
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let mut map = TriHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Person {
    id: 1,
    email: "alice@example.com".to_string(),
    phone: "555-1234".to_string(),
    name: "Alice".to_string(),
})
.unwrap();
// All three keys must match
assert_eq!(
    map.get_unique(&1, &"alice@example.com", &"555-1234").unwrap().name,
    "Alice"
);
// If any key doesn't match, returns None
assert!(map.get_unique(&1, &"wrong@example.com", &"555-1234").is_none());
assert!(map.get_unique(&2, &"alice@example.com", &"555-1234").is_none());
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp.rs.html#1737-1765)

Gets a mutable reference to the unique item associated with the given

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-24)Examples

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Person {
    id: u32,
    email: String,
    phone: String,
    name: String,
}
impl TriHashItem for Person {

    type K2<'a> = &'a str;

        self.id
    }

    }

    }

#### pub fn [remove_unique](https://docs.rs#method.remove_unique)<'a, Q1, Q2, Q3>(
    &'a mut self,
    key1: [&Q1](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    key2: [&Q2](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    key3: [&Q3](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<T>

Removes the item uniquely identified by `key1`, `key2`, and `key3`, if
it exists.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-25)Examples

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Person {
    id: u32,
    email: String,
    phone: String,
    name: String,
}
impl TriHashItem for Person {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.phone
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let mut map = TriHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Person {
    id: 1,
    email: "alice@example.com".to_string(),
    phone: "555-1234".to_string(),
    name: "Alice".to_string(),
})
.unwrap();
// Remove the item using all three keys
let removed = map.remove_unique(&1, &"alice@example.com", &"555-1234");
assert!(removed.is_some());
assert_eq!(removed.unwrap().name, "Alice");
// Map is now empty
assert!(map.is_empty());
// Trying to remove again returns None
assert!(map.remove_unique(&1, &"alice@example.com", &"555-1234").is_none());
```

        &self.phone
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let mut map = TriHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Person {
    id: 1,
    email: "alice@example.com".to_string(),
    phone: "555-1234".to_string(),
    name: "Alice".to_string(),
})
.unwrap();
let removed = map.remove3("555-1234");
assert!(removed.is_some());
assert_eq!(removed.unwrap().name, "Alice");
assert!(map.is_empty());
```
Retains only the elements specified by the predicate.

In other words, remove all items `T` for which `f(RefMut<T>)` returns
false. The elements are visited in an arbitrary order.

The `RefMut<T, S>` wrapper allows mutable access to the item while
enforcing that the three keys (`K1`, `K2`, `K3`) remain unchanged. If
a key is modified during iteration, the method will panic.

[§](https://docs.rs#performance-considerations)Performance considerations

This method may leave the internal storage fragmented. If you need
compact storage afterward, call `make_compact()`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-38)Examples

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    code: String,
    value: u32,
}
impl TriHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.code
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let mut map = TriHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Item {
    id: 1,
    name: "foo".to_string(),
    code: "x".to_string(),
    value: 42,
})
.unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item {
    id: 2,
    name: "bar".to_string(),
    code: "y".to_string(),
    value: 20,
})
.unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Item {
    id: 3,
    name: "baz".to_string(),
    code: "z".to_string(),
    value: 99,
})
.unwrap();
// Retain only items where value is greater than 30
map.retain(|item| item.value > 30);
assert_eq!(map.len(), 2);
assert_eq!(map.get1(&1).unwrap().value, 42);
assert_eq!(map.get1(&3).unwrap().value, 99);
assert!(map.get1(&2).is_none());
```

### impl<'de, T, S: [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html) + [Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html), A: [Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) + [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html)> [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)<'de> for [TriHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.TriHashMap.html)<T, S, A>

**crate feature**only.

`serde`The `Deserialize` impl for `TriHashMap` deserializes from either a sequence
or a map of items, then rebuilds the indexes and produces an error if there
are any duplicates.

In case a map is deserialized, the key is not deserialized or verified against the value. (In general, verification is not possible because the key type has a lifetime parameter embedded in it.)

The `fmt::Debug` bound on `T` ensures better error reporting.

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    email: String,
}
impl TriHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let items = vec![
    Item {
        id: 1,
        name: "foo".to_string(),
        email: "foo@example.com".to_string(),
    },
    Item {
        id: 2,
        name: "bar".to_string(),
        email: "bar@example.com".to_string(),
    },
    Item {
        id: 1,
        name: "baz".to_string(),
        email: "baz@example.com".to_string(),
    }, // overwrites first item
];
let map: TriHashMap<Item> = items.into_iter().collect();
assert_eq!(map.len(), 2);
assert_eq!(map.get1(&1).unwrap().name, "baz"); // overwritten
assert_eq!(map.get1(&1).unwrap().email, "baz@example.com");
assert_eq!(map.get1(&2).unwrap().name, "bar");
```

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-TriHashMap%3CT,+S,+A%3E)

### impl<T, S: [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html), A: [Allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator-api2/0.2.21/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/allocator_api2/stable/alloc/trait.Allocator.html)> [Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html) for [TriHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.TriHashMap.html)<T, S, A>

**crate feature**only.

`serde`A `TriHashMap` serializes to the list of items. Items are serialized in
arbitrary order.

Serializing as a list of items rather than as a map works around the lack of non-string keys in formats like JSON.

To serialize as a map instead, see [ TriHashMapAsMap](https://docs.rs/tri_hash_map/struct.TriHashMapAsMap.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-40)Examples

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Debug, Serialize)]
struct Item {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    email: String,
    value: usize,
}
// This is a complex key, so it can't be a JSON map key.
#[derive(Eq, Hash, PartialEq)]
struct ComplexKey<'a> {
    name: &'a str,
    email: &'a str,
}
impl TriHashItem for Item {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = ComplexKey<'a>;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        ComplexKey { name: &self.name, email: &self.email }
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let mut map = TriHashMap::<Item>::new();
map.insert_unique(Item {
    id: 1,
    name: "Alice".to_string(),
    email: "alice@example.com".to_string(),
    value: 42,
})
.unwrap();
// The map is serialized as a list of items.
let serialized = serde_json::to_string(&map).unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    serialized,
    r#"[{"id":1,"name":"Alice","email":"alice@example.com","value":42}]"#,
);
```

An element stored in an [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdOrdMap.html).

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
// Define a struct with a key.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct MyItem {
    id: String,
    value: u32,
}
// Implement IdOrdItem for the struct.
impl IdOrdItem for MyItem {
    // Keys can borrow from the item.
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
// Create an IdOrdMap and insert items.

map.insert_unique(MyItem { id: "foo".to_string(), value: 42 }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(MyItem { id: "bar".to_string(), value: 20 }).unwrap();

use iddqd::{BiHashItem, BiHashMap, bi_upcast};
// Define a struct with two keys.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct MyPair {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
}
// Implement BiHashItem for the struct.
impl BiHashItem for MyPair {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
// Create a BiHashMap and insert items.
let mut map = BiHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(MyPair { id: 1, name: "Alice".to_string() }).unwrap();
map.insert_unique(MyPair { id: 2, name: "Bob".to_string() }).unwrap();
```

}## Expand description

An item in a [ TriHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.TriHashMap.html).

This trait is used to define the keys.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, TriHashMap, tri_upcast};
// Define a struct with three keys.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct Person {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    email: String,
}
// Implement TriHashItem for the struct.
impl TriHashItem for Person {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
// Create a TriHashMap and insert items.
let mut map = TriHashMap::new();
map.insert_unique(Person {
    id: 1,
    name: "Alice".to_string(),
    email: "alice@example.com".to_string(),
})
.unwrap();
map.insert_unique(Person {
    id: 2,
    name: "Bob".to_string(),
    email: "bob@example.com".to_string(),
})
.unwrap();
```

# bi_hash_map in iddqd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.5/iddqd/macro.bi_hash_map.html

```
macro_rules! bi_hash_map {
    ($($item:expr,)+) => { ... };
    ($($item:expr),*) => { ... };
    ($H:ty; $($item:expr,)+) => { ... };
    ($H:ty; $($item:expr),*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Creates a [ BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.BiHashMap.html) from a list of items.

An optional [ BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html) that implements

`Default` can be provided as the first argument, followed by a semicolon.[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the list of items has duplicate keys. For better error handling,
the item is required to implement `Debug`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use iddqd::{BiHashItem, bi_hash_map, bi_upcast};
#[derive(Debug)]
struct User {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
}
impl BiHashItem for User {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    bi_upcast!();
}
let map = bi_hash_map! {
    User { id: 1, name: "Alice".to_string() },
    User { id: 2, name: "Bob".to_string() },
};
assert_eq!(map.get1(&1).unwrap().name, "Alice");
assert_eq!(map.get2("Bob").unwrap().id, 2);
// With a custom hasher:
let map = bi_hash_map! {
    foldhash::quality::RandomState;
    User { id: 3, name: "Charlie".to_string() },
    User { id: 4, name: "Eve".to_string() },
};
assert_eq!(map.get1(&3).unwrap().name, "Charlie");
assert_eq!(map.get2("Eve").unwrap().id, 4);
```

# tri_hash_map in iddqd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.5/iddqd/macro.tri_hash_map.html

```
macro_rules! tri_hash_map {
    ($($item:expr,)+) => { ... };
    ($($item:expr),*) => { ... };
    ($H:ty; $($item:expr,)+) => { ... };
    ($H:ty; $($item:expr),*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Creates a [ TriHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.TriHashMap.html) from a list of items.

An optional [ BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html) that implements

`Default` can be provided as the first argument, followed by a semicolon.[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the list of items has duplicate keys. For better error handling,
the item is required to implement `Debug`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use iddqd::{TriHashItem, tri_hash_map, tri_upcast};
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Person {
    id: u32,
    name: String,
    email: String,
}
impl TriHashItem for Person {
    type K1<'a> = u32;
    type K2<'a> = &'a str;
    type K3<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key1(&self) -> Self::K1<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    fn key2(&self) -> Self::K2<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    fn key3(&self) -> Self::K3<'_> {
        &self.email
    }
    tri_upcast!();
}
let map = tri_hash_map! {
    Person { id: 1, name: "Alice".to_string(), email: "alice@example.com".to_string() },
    Person { id: 2, name: "Bob".to_string(), email: "bob@example.com".to_string() },
};
assert_eq!(map.get1(&1).unwrap().name, "Alice");
assert_eq!(map.get2("Bob").unwrap().id, 2);
assert_eq!(map.get3("alice@example.com").unwrap().name, "Alice");
// With a custom hasher:
let map = tri_hash_map! {
    foldhash::quality::RandomState;
    Person { id: 3, name: "Charlie".to_string(), email: "charlie@example.com".to_string() },
    Person { id: 4, name: "Eve".to_string(), email: "eve@example.com".to_string() },
};
assert_eq!(map.get1(&3).unwrap().name, "Charlie");
assert_eq!(map.get2("Eve").unwrap().id, 4);
```

# iddqd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/iddqd/latest/iddqd/

## Expand description

Maps where keys are borrowed from values.

This crate consists of several map types, collectively called **ID maps**:

- `IdOrdMap`
- `IdHashMap`
- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

- Pick your ID map type.
- Depending on the ID map type, implement `IdOrdItem``IdHashItem``BiHashItem``TriHashItem`
- Store values in the ID map type.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

This crate was built out a practical need for map types, and addresses issues encountered using Rust’s default map types in practice at Oxide.

- Keys are retrieved from values, not stored separately from them. Separate storage has been a recurring pain point in our codebases: if keys are duplicated within values, it’s proven to be hard to maintain consistency between keys and values. This crate addresses that need.
- Keys may be borrowed from values, which allows for more flexible implementations. (They don’t have to be borrowed, but they can be.)
- There’s no `insert`method; insertion must be through either`insert_overwrite`or`insert_unique`. You must pick an insertion behavior.
- For hash maps, the default hasher is `foldhash`*not provide the same level of HashDoS resistance*as SipHash. If that is important to you, you can use a different hasher. (Disable the`default-hasher`feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed in.)
- The serde implementations reject duplicate keys.

We’ve also sometimes needed to index a set of data by more than one key, or
perhaps map one key to another. For that purpose, this crate provides
[ BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.BiHashMap.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.TriHashMap.html)

`TriHashMap`- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

As a consequence of the general API structure, maps can have arbitrary non-key data associated with them as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

An example for [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdOrdMap.html):

```
use iddqd::{IdOrdItem, IdOrdMap, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug)]
struct User {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
}
// Implement IdOrdItem so the map knows how to get the key from the value.
impl IdOrdItem for User {
    // The key type can borrow from the value.
    type Key<'a> = &'a str;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        &self.name
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
let mut users = IdOrdMap::<User>::new();
// You must pick an insertion behavior. insert_unique returns an error if
// the key already exists.
users.insert_unique(User { name: "Alice".to_string(), age: 30 }).unwrap();
users.insert_unique(User { name: "Bob".to_string(), age: 35 }).unwrap();
// Lookup by name:
assert_eq!(users.get("Alice").unwrap().age, 30);
assert_eq!(users.get("Bob").unwrap().age, 35);
// Iterate over users:
for user in &users {
    println!("User {}: {}", user.name, user.age);
}
```
Keys don’t have to be borrowed from the value. For smaller `Copy` types,
it’s recommended that you use owned keys. Here’s an example of using
[ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdOrdMap.html) with a small integer key:

```
struct Record {
    id: u32,
    data: String,
}
impl IdOrdItem for Record {
    // The key type is small, so an owned key is preferred.
    type Key<'a> = u32;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        self.id
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
// ...
```
An example for [ IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdHashMap.html), showing a complex borrowed key. Here,
“complex” means that the key is not a reference itself, but a struct that
returns references to more than one field from the value.

```
use iddqd::{IdHashItem, id_hash_map, id_upcast};
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Artifact {
    name: String,
    version: String,
    data: Vec<u8>,
}
// The key type is a borrowed form of the name and version. It needs to
// implement `Eq + Hash`.
#[derive(Eq, Hash, PartialEq)]
struct ArtifactKey<'a> {
    name: &'a str,
    version: &'a str,
}
impl IdHashItem for Artifact {
    // The key type can borrow from the value.
    type Key<'a> = ArtifactKey<'a>;
    fn key(&self) -> Self::Key<'_> {
        ArtifactKey { name: &self.name, version: &self.version }
    }
    id_upcast!();
}
// Create a new `IdHashMap` with the given artifacts. This uses the
// `id_hash_map!` macro that comes with iddqd.
let artifacts = id_hash_map! {
    Artifact {
        name: "artifact1".to_owned(),
        version: "1.0".to_owned(),
        data: b"data1".to_vec(),
    },
    Artifact {
        name: "artifact2".to_owned(),
        version: "1.0".to_owned(),
        data: b"data2".to_vec(),
    },
};
// Look up artifacts by name and version.
assert_eq!(
    artifacts
        .get(&ArtifactKey { name: "artifact1", version: "1.0" })
        .unwrap()
        .data,
    b"data1",
);
```
For more examples, see the
[examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd/examples)
and [extended
examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples)
directories.

[§](https://docs.rs#equivalent-and-comparable)`Equivalent` and `Comparable`

An important feature of the standard library’s maps is that they allow any
borrowed form of the key type to be used for lookups; for example, a
`HashMap<String, T>` type can be looked up with a `&str` key. This is done
through the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait.

But the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait is a bit too restrictive for complex keys such as

`ArtifactKey` above, requiring workarounds such as [dynamic dispatch](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example). To address this, the crates.io ecosystem has standardized on the

[and](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html)

`Equivalent`[traits as generalizations of](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable``Borrow`. The map types in
this crate require these traits.For a key type `T::Key<'_>` and a query type `Q`:

- The hash map types require `Q: Hash + Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. Also,`Q`must hash in the same way as`T::Key<'_>`. Typically, this is done by ensuring that enum variants and struct fields are in the same order[1](https://docs.rs#fn1)
- `IdOrdMap`- `Q: Comparable<T::Key<'_>>`, which in turn requires- `Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. (There’s no need for- `Q`to implement- `Ord`or- `Eq`itself.)

Continuing the `ArtifactKey` example from above, we can perform a lookup
using a key of this owned form:

```
use equivalent::Equivalent;
// This is an owned form of ArtifactKey. The fields are in the same
// order as ArtifactKey's fields, so it hashes the same way.
#[derive(Hash)]
struct OwnedArtifactKey {
    name: String,
    version: String,
}
impl Equivalent<ArtifactKey<'_>> for OwnedArtifactKey {
    fn equivalent(&self, other: &ArtifactKey<'_>) -> bool {
        self.name == other.name && self.version == other.version
    }
}
// Now you can use OwnedArtifactKey to look up the artifact.
let owned_key = OwnedArtifactKey {
    name: "artifact1".to_owned(),
    version: "1.0".to_owned(),
};
assert_eq!(artifacts.get(&owned_key).unwrap().data, b"data1",);
```
There’s a blanket implementation of [ Equivalent](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html) and

[for](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable`[, so if your type already implements](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`[, there aren’t any extra steps to take.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`[§](https://docs.rs#testing-and-verification)Testing and verification

This crate is validated through a combination of:

- Unit tests
- Property-based tests using a naive map as an oracle
- Unit and property-based tests for several kinds of pathological `Eq`,`Hash`and`Ord`implementations
- Property-based tests for panic safety
- Miri tests for unsafe code, checked against both Stacked and Tree Borrows
- Compile-fail UI tests to ensure invalid patterns are rejected by the borrow checker
- Bounded formal verification for core invariants and UB using
[Soteria](https://soteria-tools.com)

Pathological user implementations written in safe Rust might corrupt internal map state and result in panics, but should never cause UB.

For more information on our validation philosophy, see [this Oxide blog
entry](https://oxide.computer/blog/iddqd-unsafe).

If you see a gap in testing, new tests are welcome. Thank you!

Note that **testing requires  cargo-nextest**: several
tests depend on nextest’s process-per-test model.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-compatibility)No-std compatibility

Most of this crate is no-std compatible, though [ alloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/index.html) is required.

The [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/struct.IdOrdMap.html) type is not currently no-std compatible due to its use of a
thread-local. This thread-local is just a way to work around a limitation in
std’s

`BTreeMap` API, though. Either a custom B-Tree implementation, or a
platform-specific notion of thread locals, would suffice to make
[no-std compatible.](https://docs.rs/struct.IdOrdMap.html)

# allocator-api2 0.2.21 - Docs.rs

# allocator-api2

This crate mirrors types and traits from Rust's unstable [ allocator_api](https://doc.rust-lang.org/unstable-book/library-features/allocator-api.html)
The intention of this crate is to serve as substitution for actual thing
for libs when build on stable and beta channels.
The target users are library authors who implement allocators or collection types
that use allocators, or anyone else who wants using

`allocator_api`The crate should be frequently updated with minor version bump.
When [ allocator_api](https://doc.rust-lang.org/unstable-book/library-features/allocator-api.html) is stable this crate will get version

`1.0` and simply
re-export from `core`, `alloc` and `std`.The code is mostly verbatim copy from rust repository. Mostly attributes are removed.

## Usage

This paragraph describes how to use this crate correctly to ensure compatibility and interoperability on both stable and nightly channels.

If you are writing a library that interacts with allocators API, you can
add this crate as a dependency and use the types and traits from this
crate instead of the ones in `core` or `alloc`.
This will allow your library to compile on stable and beta channels.

Your library *MAY* provide a feature that will enable "allocator-api2/nightly".
When this feature is enabled, your library *MUST* enable
unstable `#![feature(allocator_api)]` or it may not compile.
If feature is not provided, your library may not be compatible with the
rest of the users and cause compilation errors on nightly channel
when some other crate enables "allocator-api2/nightly" feature.

# Minimal Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate is guaranteed to compile on stable Rust 1.63 and up. A feature "fresh-rust" bumps the MSRV to unspecified higher version, but should be compatible with at least few latest stable releases. The feature enables some additional functionality:

- `CStr`without "std" feature
