# iddqd 0.4.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/iddqd/0.4.2

# iddqd

Maps where keys are borrowed from values.

This crate consists of several map types, collectively called **ID maps**:

- `IdOrdMap`
- `IdHashMap`
- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

## Usage

- Pick your ID map type.
- Depending on the ID map type, implement `IdOrdItem``IdHashItem``BiHashItem``TriHashItem`
- Store values in the ID map type.

### Features

This crate was built out a practical need for map types, and addresses issues encountered using Rust’s default map types in practice at Oxide.

- Keys are retrieved from values, not stored separately from them. Separate storage has been a recurring pain point in our codebases: if keys are duplicated within values, it’s proven to be hard to maintain consistency between keys and values. This crate addresses that need.
- Keys may be borrowed from values, which allows for more flexible implementations. (They don’t have to be borrowed, but they can be.)
- There’s no `insert`method; insertion must be through either`insert_overwrite`or`insert_unique`. You must pick an insertion behavior.
- For hash maps, the default hasher is `foldhash`*not provide the same level of HashDoS resistance*as SipHash. If that is important to you, you can use a different hasher. (Disable the`default-hasher`feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed in.)
- The serde implementations reject duplicate keys.

We’ve also sometimes needed to index a set of data by more than one key, or
perhaps map one key to another. For that purpose, this crate provides
[ BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.2/iddqd/bi_hash_map/imp/struct.BiHashMap.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.2/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp/struct.TriHashMap.html)

`TriHashMap`- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

As a consequence of the general API structure, maps can have arbitrary non-key data associated with them as well.

### Examples

An example for [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.2/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html):

```
use ;
// Implement IdOrdItem so the map knows how to get the key from the value.
let mut users = new;
// You must pick an insertion behavior. insert_unique returns an error if
// the key already exists.
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
// Lookup by name:
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// Iterate over users:
for user in &users
```
Keys don’t have to be borrowed from the value. For smaller `Copy` types,
it’s recommended that you use owned keys. Here’s an example of using
[ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.2/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) with a small integer key:

```
// ...
```
An example for [ IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.2/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp/struct.IdHashMap.html), showing a complex borrowed key. Here,
“complex” means that the key is not a reference itself, but a struct that
returns references to more than one field from the value.

```
use ;
// The key type is a borrowed form of the name and version. It needs to
// implement `Eq + Hash`.
// Create a new `IdHashMap` with the given artifacts. This uses the
// `id_hash_map!` macro that comes with iddqd.
let artifacts = id_hash_map! ;
// Look up artifacts by name and version.
assert_eq!;
```
For more examples, see the
[examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd/examples)
and [extended
examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples)
directories.

`Equivalent` and `Comparable`

An important feature of the standard library’s maps is that they allow any
borrowed form of the key type to be used for lookups; for example, a
`HashMap<String, T>` type can be looked up with a `&str` key. This is done
through the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait.

But the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait is a bit too restrictive for complex keys such as

`ArtifactKey` above, requiring workarounds such as [dynamic dispatch](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example). To address this, the crates.io ecosystem has standardized on the

[and](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html)

`Equivalent`[traits as generalizations of](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable``Borrow`. The map types in
this crate require these traits.For a key type `T::Key<'_>` and a lookup type `L`:

- The hash map types require `L: Hash + Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. Also,`L`must hash in the same way as`T::Key<'_>`. Typically, this is done by ensuring that enum variants and struct fields are in the same order[^proptest].
- `IdOrdMap`- `L: Comparable<T::Key<'_>>`, which in turn requires- `Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. (There’s no need for- `L`to implement- `Ord`or- `Eq`itself.)

[^proptest]: We recommend that you test this with e.g. a property-based
test: see [this
example](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example/blob/a6f17699/src/lib.rs#L233).

Continuing the `ArtifactKey` example from above, we can perform a lookup
using a key of this owned form:

```
use Equivalent;
// This is an owned form of ArtifactKey. The fields are in the same
// order as ArtifactKey's fields, so it hashes the same way.
// Now you can use OwnedArtifactKey to look up the artifact.
let owned_key = OwnedArtifactKey ;
assert_eq!;
```
There’s a blanket implementation of [ Equivalent](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html) and

[for](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable`[, so if your type already implements](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`[, there aren’t any extra steps to take.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`## Testing

This crate is validated through a combination of:

- Unit tests
- Property-based tests using a naive map as an oracle
- Unit and property-based tests for several kinds of pathological `Eq`,`Hash`and`Ord`implementations
- Property-based tests for panic safety
- Miri tests for unsafe code, checked against both Stacked and Tree Borrows
- Compile-fail UI tests to ensure invalid patterns are rejected by the borrow checker

Pathological user implementations written in safe Rust might corrupt internal map state and result in panics, but should never cause UB.

If you see a gap in testing, new tests are welcome. Thank you!

Note that **testing requires  cargo-nextest**: several
tests depend on nextest’s process-per-test model.

## No-std compatibility

Most of this crate is no-std compatible, though [ alloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/index.html) is required.

The [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.2/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) type is not currently no-std compatible due to its use of a
thread-local. This thread-local is just a way to work around a limitation in
std’s

`BTreeMap` API, though. Either a custom B-Tree implementation, or a
platform-specific notion of thread locals, would suffice to make
[no-std compatible.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.2/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html)

`IdOrdMap`## Optional features

- `allocator-api2`: Enables support for custom allocators via the- `allocator_api2`- `bumpalo`) are supported. Custom allocators are not currently supported by- `IdOrdMap`.
- `daft`: Enables- `daft`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `default-hasher`: Enables the- `DefaultHashBuilder`type. Disable this feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed into- `IdHashMap`- `BiHashMap`- `TriHashMap`- *Enabled by default.*
- `proptest`: Enables- `proptest`- `Arbitrary`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `schemars08`: Enables- `schemars`- [automatic replacement](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/blob/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples/typify-types.rs)through- `typify`- `dropshot`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `serde`: Enables serde support for all ID map types.- *Not enabled by default.*
- `std`: Enables std support.- *Enabled by default.*

## Related work

-
`bimap`
-
`multi_index_map``Clone`. In`iddqd`, we pick a somewhat different point in the design space, but we think`multi_index_map`is also great.
-
In general, this is similar to relational database records with indexes. For sufficiently complex use cases, consider an embedded database like [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/), or even a networked database like[PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/).`iddqd`is a good fit for simple in-memory caches of data stored in these databases.

## Minimum supported Rust version (MSRV)

This crate’s MSRV is **Rust 1.85**. In general we aim for 6 months of Rust
compatibility.

## What does iddqd mean?

The name `iddqd` is a reference to [a cheat
code](https://doomwiki.org/wiki/Doom_cheat_codes) in the classic video game
*Doom*. It has `id` in the name, and is short and memorable.

license](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT).

- Unit and property-based tests for several kinds of pathological `Eq`,`Hash`and`Ord`implementations
- Property-based tests for panic safety
- Miri tests for unsafe code, checked against both Stacked and Tree Borrows

Pathological user implementations written in safe Rust might corrupt internal map state and result in panics, but should never cause UB.

If you see a gap in testing, new tests are welcome. Thank you!

Note that **testing requires  cargo-nextest**: several
tests depend on nextest’s process-per-test model.

## No-std compatibility

Most of this crate is no-std compatible, though [ alloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/index.html) is required.

The [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.0/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) type is not currently no-std compatible due to its use of a
thread-local. This thread-local is just a way to work around a limitation in
std’s

`BTreeMap` API, though. Either a custom B-Tree implementation, or a
platform-specific notion of thread locals, would suffice to make
[no-std compatible.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.4.0/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html)

`IdOrdMap`## Optional features

- `allocator-api2`: Enables support for custom allocators via the- `allocator_api2`- `bumpalo`) are supported. Custom allocators are not currently supported by- `IdOrdMap`.
- `daft`: Enables- `daft`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `default-hasher`: Enables the- `DefaultHashBuilder`type. Disable this feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed into- `IdHashMap`- `BiHashMap`- `TriHashMap`- *Enabled by default.*
- `proptest`: Enables- `proptest`- `Arbitrary`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `schemars08`: Enables- `schemars`- [automatic replacement](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/blob/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples/typify-types.rs)through- `typify`- `dropshot`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `serde`: Enables serde support for all ID map types.- *Not enabled by default.*
- `std`: Enables std support.- *Enabled by default.*

## Related work

-
`bimap`
-
`multi_index_map``Clone`. In`iddqd`, we pick a somewhat different point in the design space, but we think`multi_index_map`is also great.
-
In general, this is similar to relational database records with indexes. For sufficiently complex use cases, consider an embedded database like [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/), or even a networked database like[PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/).`iddqd`is a good fit for simple in-memory caches of data stored in these databases.

# iddqd 0.3.18 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/iddqd/0.3.18

# iddqd

Maps where keys are borrowed from values.

This crate consists of several map types, collectively called **ID maps**:

- `IdOrdMap`
- `IdHashMap`
- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

## Usage

- Pick your ID map type.
- Depending on the ID map type, implement `IdOrdItem``IdHashItem``BiHashItem``TriHashItem`
- Store values in the ID map type.

### Features

This crate was built out a practical need for map types, and addresses issues encountered using Rust’s default map types in practice at Oxide.

- Keys are retrieved from values, not stored separately from them. Separate storage has been a recurring pain point in our codebases: if keys are duplicated within values, it’s proven to be hard to maintain consistency between keys and values. This crate addresses that need.
- Keys may be borrowed from values, which allows for more flexible implementations. (They don’t have to be borrowed, but they can be.)
- There’s no `insert`method; insertion must be through either`insert_overwrite`or`insert_unique`. You must pick an insertion behavior.
- For hash maps, the default hasher is `foldhash`*not provide the same level of HashDoS resistance*as SipHash. If that is important to you, you can use a different hasher. (Disable the`default-hasher`feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed in.)
- The serde implementations reject duplicate keys.

We’ve also sometimes needed to index a set of data by more than one key, or
perhaps map one key to another. For that purpose, this crate provides
[ BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.18/iddqd/bi_hash_map/imp/struct.BiHashMap.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.18/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp/struct.TriHashMap.html)

`TriHashMap`- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

As a consequence of the general API structure, maps can have arbitrary non-key data associated with them as well.

### Examples

An example for [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.18/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html):

```
use ;
// Implement IdOrdItem so the map knows how to get the key from the value.
let mut users = new;
// You must pick an insertion behavior. insert_unique returns an error if
// the key already exists.
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
// Lookup by name:
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// Iterate over users:
for user in &users
```
Keys don’t have to be borrowed from the value. For smaller `Copy` types,
it’s recommended that you use owned keys. Here’s an example of using
[ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.18/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) with a small integer key:

```
// ...
```
An example for [ IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.18/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp/struct.IdHashMap.html), showing a complex borrowed key. Here,
“complex” means that the key is not a reference itself, but a struct that
returns references to more than one field from the value.

```
use ;
// The key type is a borrowed form of the name and version. It needs to
// implement `Eq + Hash`.
// Create a new `IdHashMap` with the given artifacts. This uses the
// `id_hash_map!` macro that comes with iddqd.
let artifacts = id_hash_map! ;
// Look up artifacts by name and version.
assert_eq!;
```
For more examples, see the
[examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd/examples)
and [extended
examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples)
directories.

`Equivalent` and `Comparable`

An important feature of the standard library’s maps is that they allow any
borrowed form of the key type to be used for lookups; for example, a
`HashMap<String, T>` type can be looked up with a `&str` key. This is done
through the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait.

But the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait is a bit too restrictive for complex keys such as

`ArtifactKey` above, requiring workarounds such as [dynamic dispatch](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example). To address this, the crates.io ecosystem has standardized on the

[and](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html)

`Equivalent`[traits as generalizations of](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable``Borrow`. The map types in
this crate require these traits.For a key type `T::Key<'_>` and a lookup type `L`:

- The hash map types require `L: Hash + Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. Also,`L`must hash in the same way as`T::Key<'_>`. Typically, this is done by ensuring that enum variants and struct fields are in the same order[^proptest].
- `IdOrdMap`- `L: Comparable<T::Key<'_>>`, which in turn requires- `Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. (There’s no need for- `L`to implement- `Ord`or- `Eq`itself.)

[^proptest]: We recommend that you test this with e.g. a property-based
test: see [this
example](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example/blob/a6f17699/src/lib.rs#L233).

Continuing the `ArtifactKey` example from above, we can perform a lookup
using a key of this owned form:

```
use Equivalent;
// This is an owned form of ArtifactKey. The fields are in the same
// order as ArtifactKey's fields, so it hashes the same way.
// Now you can use OwnedArtifactKey to look up the artifact.
let owned_key = OwnedArtifactKey ;
assert_eq!;
```
There’s a blanket implementation of [ Equivalent](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html) and

[for](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable`[, so if your type already implements](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`[, there aren’t any extra steps to take.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`## Testing

This crate is validated through a combination of:

- Unit tests
- Property-based tests using a naive map as an oracle
- Chaos tests for several kinds of buggy `Eq`and`Ord`implementations
- Miri tests for unsafe code

If you see a gap in testing, new tests are welcome. Thank you!

## No-std compatibility

thread-local. This thread-local is just a way to work around a limitation in
std’s

`BTreeMap` API, though. Either a custom B-Tree implementation, or a
platform-specific notion of thread locals, would suffice to make
[no-std compatible.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.18/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html)

`IdOrdMap`## Optional features

- `allocator-api2`: Enables support for custom allocators via the- `allocator_api2`- `bumpalo`) are supported. Custom allocators are not currently supported by- `IdOrdMap`.
- `daft`: Enables- `daft`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `default-hasher`: Enables the- `DefaultHashBuilder`type. Disable this feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed into- `IdHashMap`- `BiHashMap`- `TriHashMap`- *Enabled by default.*
- `proptest`: Enables- `proptest`- `Arbitrary`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `schemars08`: Enables- `schemars`- [automatic replacement](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/blob/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples/typify-types.rs)through- `typify`- `dropshot`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `serde`: Enables serde support for all ID map types.- *Not enabled by default.*
- `std`: Enables std support.- *Enabled by default.*

## Related work

-
`bimap`
-
`multi_index_map``Clone`. In`iddqd`, we pick a somewhat different point in the design space, but we think`multi_index_map`is also great.
-

For sufficiently complex use cases, consider an embedded database like [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/), or even a networked database like[PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/).`iddqd`is a good fit for simple in-memory caches of data stored in these databases.

`ArtifactKey` above, requiring workarounds such as [dynamic dispatch](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example). To address this, the crates.io ecosystem has standardized on the

[and](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html)

`Equivalent`[traits as generalizations of](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable``Borrow`. The map types in
this crate require these traits.For a key type `T::Key<'_>` and a lookup type `L`:

- The hash map types require `L: Hash + Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. Also,`L`must hash in the same way as`T::Key<'_>`. Typically, this is done by ensuring that enum variants and struct fields are in the same order[^proptest].
- `IdOrdMap`- `L: Comparable<T::Key<'_>>`, which in turn requires- `Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. (There’s no need for- `L`to implement- `Ord`or- `Eq`itself.)

[^proptest]: We recommend that you test this with e.g. a property-based
test: see [this
example](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example/blob/a6f17699/src/lib.rs#L233).

Continuing the `ArtifactKey` example from above, we can perform a lookup
using a key of this owned form:

```
use Equivalent;
// This is an owned form of ArtifactKey. The fields are in the same
// order as ArtifactKey's fields, so it hashes the same way.
// Now you can use OwnedArtifactKey to look up the artifact.
let owned_key = OwnedArtifactKey ;
assert_eq!;
```
There’s a blanket implementation of [ Equivalent](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html) and

[for](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable`[, so if your type already implements](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`[, there aren’t any extra steps to take.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`## Testing

This crate is validated through a combination of:

- Unit tests
- Property-based tests using a naive map as an oracle
- Chaos tests for several kinds of buggy `Eq`and`Ord`implementations
- Miri tests for unsafe code

If you see a gap in testing, new tests are welcome. Thank you!

## No-std compatibility

Most of this crate is no-std compatible, though [ alloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/index.html) is required.

The [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.16/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) type is not currently no-std compatible due to its use of a
thread-local. This thread-local is just a way to work around a limitation in
std’s

`BTreeMap` API, though. Either a custom B-Tree implementation, or a
platform-specific notion of thread locals, would suffice to make
[no-std compatible.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.16/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html)

`IdOrdMap`## Optional features

- `allocator-api2`: Enables support for custom allocators via the- `allocator_api2`- `bumpalo`) are supported. Custom allocators are not currently supported by- `IdOrdMap`.
- `daft`: Enables- `daft`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `default-hasher`: Enables the- `DefaultHashBuilder`type. Disable this feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed into- `IdHashMap`- `BiHashMap`- `TriHashMap`- *Enabled by default.*
- `proptest`: Enables- `proptest`- `Arbitrary`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `schemars08`: Enables- `schemars`- [automatic replacement](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/blob/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples/typify-types.rs)through- `typify`- `dropshot`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `serde`: Enables serde support for all ID map types.- *Not enabled by default.*
- `std`: Enables std support.- *Enabled by default.*

## Related work

-
`bimap`
-
`multi_index_map``Clone`. In`iddqd`, we pick a somewhat different point in the design space, but we think`multi_index_map`is also great.
-
In general, this is similar to relational database records with indexes. For sufficiently complex use cases, consider an embedded database like [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/), or even a networked database like[PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/).`iddqd`is a good fit for simple in-memory caches of data stored in these databases.

# iddqd 0.3.15 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/iddqd/0.3.15

# iddqd

Maps where keys are borrowed from values.

This crate consists of several map types, collectively called **ID maps**:

- `IdOrdMap`
- `IdHashMap`
- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

## Usage

- Pick your ID map type.
- Depending on the ID map type, implement `IdOrdItem``IdHashItem``BiHashItem``TriHashItem`
- Store values in the ID map type.

### Features

This crate was built out a practical need for map types, and addresses issues encountered using Rust’s default map types in practice at Oxide.

- Keys are retrieved from values, not stored separately from them. Separate storage has been a recurring pain point in our codebases: if keys are duplicated within values, it’s proven to be hard to maintain consistency between keys and values. This crate addresses that need.
- Keys may be borrowed from values, which allows for more flexible implementations. (They don’t have to be borrowed, but they can be.)
- There’s no `insert`method; insertion must be through either`insert_overwrite`or`insert_unique`. You must pick an insertion behavior.
- For hash maps, the default hasher is `foldhash`*not provide the same level of HashDoS resistance*as SipHash. If that is important to you, you can use a different hasher. (Disable the`default-hasher`feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed in.)
- The serde implementations reject duplicate keys.

We’ve also sometimes needed to index a set of data by more than one key, or
perhaps map one key to another. For that purpose, this crate provides
[ BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.15/iddqd/bi_hash_map/imp/struct.BiHashMap.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.15/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp/struct.TriHashMap.html)

`TriHashMap`- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

As a consequence of the general API structure, maps can have arbitrary non-key data associated with them as well.

### Examples

An example for [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.15/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html):

```
use ;
// Implement IdOrdItem so the map knows how to get the key from the value.
let mut users = new;
// You must pick an insertion behavior. insert_unique returns an error if
// the key already exists.
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
// Lookup by name:
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// Iterate over users:
for user in &users
```
Keys don’t have to be borrowed from the value. For smaller `Copy` types,
it’s recommended that you use owned keys. Here’s an example of using
[ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.15/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) with a small integer key:

```
// ...
```
An example for [ IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.15/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp/struct.IdHashMap.html), showing a complex borrowed key. Here,
“complex” means that the key is not a reference itself, but a struct that
returns references to more than one field from the value.

```
use ;
// The key type is a borrowed form of the name and version. It needs to
// implement `Eq + Hash`.
// Create a new `IdHashMap` with the given artifacts. This uses the
// `id_hash_map!` macro that comes with iddqd.
let artifacts = id_hash_map! ;
// Look up artifacts by name and version.
assert_eq!;
```
For more examples, see the
[examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd/examples)
and [extended
examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples)
directories.

`Equivalent` and `Comparable`

An important feature of the standard library’s maps is that they allow any
borrowed form of the key type to be used for lookups; for example, a
`HashMap<String, T>` type can be looked up with a `&str` key. This is done
through the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait.

But the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait is a bit too restrictive for complex keys such as

- `IdOrdMap`- `L: Comparable<T::Key<'_>>`, which in turn requires- `Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. (There’s no need for- `L`to implement- `Ord`or- `Eq`itself.)

[^proptest]: We recommend that you test this with e.g. a property-based
test: see [this
example](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example/blob/a6f17699/src/lib.rs#L233).

// order as ArtifactKey's fields, so it hashes the same way.

// You must pick an insertion behavior. insert_unique returns an error if
// the key already exists.
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
// Lookup by name:
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// Iterate over users:
for user in &users
```
Keys don’t have to be borrowed from the value. For smaller `Copy` types,
it’s recommended that you use owned keys. Here’s an example of using
[ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.13/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) with a small integer key:

```
// ...
```
An example for [ IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.13/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp/struct.IdHashMap.html), showing a complex borrowed key. Here,
“complex” means that the key is not a reference itself, but a struct that
returns references to more than one field from the value.

```
use ;
// The key type is a borrowed form of the name and version. It needs to
// implement `Eq + Hash`.
// Create a new `IdHashMap` with the given artifacts. This uses the
// `id_hash_map!` macro that comes with iddqd.
let artifacts = id_hash_map! ;
// Look up artifacts by name and version.
assert_eq!;
```
For more examples, see the
[examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd/examples)
and [extended
examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples)
directories.

`Equivalent` and `Comparable`

An important feature of the standard library’s maps is that they allow any
borrowed form of the key type to be used for lookups; for example, a
`HashMap<String, T>` type can be looked up with a `&str` key. This is done
through the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait.

But the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait is a bit too restrictive for complex keys such as

`ArtifactKey` above, requiring workarounds such as [dynamic dispatch](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example). To address this, the crates.io ecosystem has standardized on the

[and](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html)

`Equivalent`[traits as generalizations of](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable``Borrow`. The map types in
this crate require these traits.For a key type `T::Key<'_>` and a lookup type `L`:

- The hash map types require `L: Hash + Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. Also,`L`must hash in the same way as`T::Key<'_>`. Typically, this is done by ensuring that enum variants and struct fields are in the same order[^proptest].
- `IdOrdMap`- `L: Comparable<T::Key<'_>>`, which in turn requires- `Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. (There’s no need for- `L`to implement- `Ord`or- `Eq`itself.)

[^proptest]: We recommend that you test this with e.g. a property-based
test: see [this
example](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example/blob/a6f17699/src/lib.rs#L233).

Continuing the `ArtifactKey` example from above, we can perform a lookup
using a key of this owned form:

```
use Equivalent;
// This is an owned form of ArtifactKey. The fields are in the same
// order as ArtifactKey's fields, so it hashes the same way.
// Now you can use OwnedArtifactKey to look up the artifact.
let owned_key = OwnedArtifactKey ;
assert_eq!;
```
There’s a blanket implementation of [ Equivalent](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html) and

[for](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable`[, so if your type already implements](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`[, there aren’t any extra steps to take.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`## Testing

This crate is validated through a combination of:

- Unit tests
- Property-based tests using a naive map as an oracle
- Chaos tests for several kinds of buggy `Eq`and`Ord`implementations
- Miri tests for unsafe code

If you see a gap in testing, new tests are welcome. Thank you!

## No-std compatibility

Most of this crate is no-std compatible, though [ alloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/index.html) is required.

The [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.13/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) type is not currently no-std compatible due to its use of a
thread-local. This thread-local is just a way to work around a limitation in
std’s

`BTreeMap` API, though. Either a custom B-Tree implementation, or a
platform-specific notion of thread locals, would suffice to make
[no-std compatible.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.13/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html)

`IdOrdMap`## Optional features

- `allocator-api2`: Enables support for custom allocators via the- `allocator_api2`- `bumpalo`) are supported. Custom allocators are not currently supported by- `IdOrdMap`.
- `daft`: Enables- `daft`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `default-hasher`: Enables the- `DefaultHashBuilder`type. Disable this feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed into- `IdHashMap`- `BiHashMap`- `TriHashMap`- *Enabled by default.*
- `proptest`: Enables- `proptest`- `Arbitrary`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `schemars08`: Enables- `schemars`- [automatic replacement](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/blob/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples/typify-types.rs)through- `typify`- `dropshot`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `serde`: Enables serde support for all ID map types.- *Not enabled by default.*
- `std`: Enables std support.- *Enabled by default.*

## Related work

-
`bimap`
-
`multi_index_map``Clone`. In`iddqd`, we pick a somewhat different point in the design space, but we think`multi_index_map`is also great.
-
In general, this is similar to relational database records with indexes. For sufficiently complex use cases, consider an embedded database like [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/), or even a networked database like[PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/).`iddqd`is a good fit for simple in-memory caches of data stored in these databases.

## Minimum supported Rust version (MSRV)

This crate’s MSRV is **Rust 1.81**. In general we aim for 6 months of Rust
compatibility.

## What does iddqd mean?

The name `iddqd` is a reference to [a cheat
code](https://doomwiki.org/wiki/Doom_cheat_codes) in the classic video game
*Doom*. It has `id` in the name, and is short and memorable.

# iddqd 0.3.12 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/iddqd/0.3.12

# iddqd

Maps where keys are borrowed from values.

This crate consists of several map types, collectively called **ID maps**:

- `IdOrdMap`
- `IdHashMap`
- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

## Usage

- Pick your ID map type.
- Depending on the ID map type, implement `IdOrdItem``IdHashItem``BiHashItem``TriHashItem`
- Store values in the ID map type.

### Features

This crate was built out a practical need for map types, and addresses issues encountered using Rust’s default map types in practice at Oxide.

- Keys are retrieved from values, not stored separately from them. Separate storage has been a recurring pain point in our codebases: if keys are duplicated within values, it’s proven to be hard to maintain consistency between keys and values. This crate addresses that need.
- Keys may be borrowed from values, which allows for more flexible implementations. (They don’t have to be borrowed, but they can be.)
- There’s no `insert`method; insertion must be through either`insert_overwrite`or`insert_unique`. You must pick an insertion behavior.
- For hash maps, the default hasher is `foldhash`*not provide the same level of HashDoS resistance*as SipHash. If that is important to you, you can use a different hasher. (Disable the`default-hasher`feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed in.)
- The serde implementations reject duplicate keys.

We’ve also sometimes needed to index a set of data by more than one key, or
perhaps map one key to another. For that purpose, this crate provides
[ BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.12/iddqd/bi_hash_map/imp/struct.BiHashMap.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.12/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp/struct.TriHashMap.html)

`TriHashMap`- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

As a consequence of the general API structure, maps can have arbitrary non-key data associated with them as well.

### Examples

An example for [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.12/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html):

```
use ;
// Implement IdOrdItem so the map knows how to get the key from the value.

// the key already exists.

```
For more examples, see the
[examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd/examples)
and [extended
examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples)

- `TriHashMap`

## Usage

- Pick your ID map type.
- Depending on the ID map type, implement `IdOrdItem``IdHashItem``BiHashItem``TriHashItem`
- Store values in the ID map type.

### Features

This crate was built out a practical need for map types, and addresses issues encountered using Rust’s default map types in practice at Oxide.

- Keys are retrieved from values, not stored separately from them. Separate storage has been a recurring pain point in our codebases: if keys are duplicated within values, it’s proven to be hard to maintain consistency between keys and values. This crate addresses that need.
- Keys may be borrowed from values, which allows for more flexible implementations. (They don’t have to be borrowed, but they can be.)
- There’s no `insert`method; insertion must be through either`insert_overwrite`or`insert_unique`. You must pick an insertion behavior.
- For hash maps, the default hasher is `foldhash`*not provide the same level of HashDoS resistance*as SipHash. If that is important to you, you can use a different hasher. (Disable the`default-hasher`feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed in.)
- The serde implementations reject duplicate keys.

We’ve also sometimes needed to index a set of data by more than one key, or
perhaps map one key to another. For that purpose, this crate provides
[ BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.10/iddqd/bi_hash_map/imp/struct.BiHashMap.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.10/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp/struct.TriHashMap.html)

`TriHashMap`- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

As a consequence of the general API structure, maps can have arbitrary non-key data associated with them as well.

### Examples

An example for [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.10/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html):

```
use ;
// Implement IdOrdItem so the map knows how to get the key from the value.
let mut users = new;
// You must pick an insertion behavior. insert_unique returns an error if
// the key already exists.
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
// Lookup by name:
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// Iterate over users:
for user in &users
```
Keys don’t have to be borrowed from the value. For smaller `Copy` types,
it’s recommended that you use owned keys. Here’s an example of using
[ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.10/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) with a small integer key:

```
// ...
```
An example for [ IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.10/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp/struct.IdHashMap.html), showing a complex borrowed key. Here,
“complex” means that the key is not a reference itself, but a struct that
returns references to more than one field from the value.

```
use ;
// The key type is a borrowed form of the name and version. It needs to
// implement `Eq + Hash`.
// Create a new `IdHashMap` with the given artifacts. This uses the
// `id_hash_map!` macro that comes with iddqd.
let artifacts = id_hash_map! ;
// Look up artifacts by name and version.
assert_eq!;
```
For more examples, see the
[examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd/examples)
and [extended
examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples)
directories.

`Equivalent` and `Comparable`

An important feature of the standard library’s maps is that they allow any
borrowed form of the key type to be used for lookups; for example, a
`HashMap<String, T>` type can be looked up with a `&str` key. This is done
through the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait.

But the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait is a bit too restrictive for complex keys such as

`ArtifactKey` above, requiring workarounds such as [dynamic dispatch](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example). To address this, the crates.io ecosystem has standardized on the

[and](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html)

`Equivalent`[traits as generalizations of](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable``Borrow`. The map types in
this crate require these traits.For a key type `T::Key<'_>` and a lookup type `L`:

- The hash map types require `L: Hash + Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. Also,`L`must hash in the same way as`T::Key<'_>`. Typically, this is done by ensuring that enum variants and struct fields are in the same order[^proptest].
- `IdOrdMap`- `L: Comparable<T::Key<'_>>`, which in turn requires- `Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. (There’s no need for- `L`to implement- `Ord`or- `Eq`itself.)

[^proptest]: We recommend that you test this with e.g. a property-based
test: see [this
example](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example/blob/a6f17699/src/lib.rs#L233).

Continuing the `ArtifactKey` example from above, we can perform a lookup
using a key of this owned form:

```
use Equivalent;
// This is an owned form of ArtifactKey. The fields are in the same
// order as ArtifactKey's fields, so it hashes the same way.
// Now you can use OwnedArtifactKey to look up the artifact.
let owned_key = OwnedArtifactKey ;
assert_eq!;
```
There’s a blanket implementation of [ Equivalent](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html) and

[for](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable`[, so if your type already implements](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`[, there aren’t any extra steps to take.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`## Testing

This crate is validated through a combination of:

- Unit tests
- Property-based tests using a naive map as an oracle
- Chaos tests for several kinds of buggy `Eq`and`Ord`implementations
- Miri tests for unsafe code

If you see a gap in testing, new tests are welcome. Thank you!

## No-std compatibility

Most of this crate is no-std compatible, though [ alloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/index.html) is required.

The [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.10/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) type is not currently no-std compatible due to its use of a
thread-local. This thread-local is just a way to work around a limitation in
std’s

`BTreeMap` API, though. Either a custom B-Tree implementation, or a
platform-specific notion of thread locals, would suffice to make
[no-std compatible.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.10/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html)

`IdOrdMap`## Optional features

- `allocator-api2`: Enables support for custom allocators via the- `allocator_api2`- `bumpalo`) are supported. Custom allocators are not currently supported by- `IdOrdMap`.
- `daft`: Enables- `daft`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `default-hasher`: Enables the- `DefaultHashBuilder`type. Disable this feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed into- `IdHashMap`- `BiHashMap`- `TriHashMap`- *Enabled by default.*
- `proptest`: Enables- `proptest`- `Arbitrary`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `schemars08`: Enables- `schemars`- [automatic replacement](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/blob/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples/typify-types.rs)through- `typify`- `dropshot`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `serde`: Enables serde support for all ID map types.- *Not enabled by default.*
- `std`: Enables std support.- *Enabled by default.*

## Related work

-
`bimap`
-
`multi_index_map``Clone`. In`iddqd`, we pick a somewhat different point in the design space, but we think`multi_index_map`is also great.
-
In general, this is similar to relational database records with indexes. For sufficiently complex use cases, consider an embedded database like [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/), or even a networked database like[PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/).`iddqd`is a good fit for simple in-memory caches of data stored in these databases.

## Minimum supported Rust version (MSRV)

This crate’s MSRV is **Rust 1.81**. In general we aim for 6 months of Rust
compatibility.

## What does iddqd mean?

The name `iddqd` is a reference to [a cheat
code](https://doomwiki.org/wiki/Doom_cheat_codes) in the classic video game
*Doom*. It has `id` in the name, and is short and memorable.

- `std`: Enables std support.- *Enabled by default.*

`bimap`
-
`multi_index_map``Clone`. In`iddqd`, we pick a somewhat different point in the design space, but we think`multi_index_map`is also great.
-

# iddqd 0.3.7 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/iddqd/0.3.7

# iddqd

Maps where keys are borrowed from values.

This crate consists of several map types, collectively called **ID maps**:

- `IdOrdMap`
- `IdHashMap`
- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

## Usage

- Pick your ID map type.
- Depending on the ID map type, implement `IdOrdItem``IdHashItem``BiHashItem``TriHashItem`
- Store values in the ID map type.

### Features

This crate was built out a practical need for map types, and addresses issues encountered using Rust’s default map types in practice at Oxide.

- Keys are retrieved from values, not stored separately from them. Separate storage has been a recurring pain point in our codebases: if keys are duplicated within values, it’s proven to be hard to maintain consistency between keys and values. This crate addresses that need.
- Keys may be borrowed from values, which allows for more flexible implementations. (They don’t have to be borrowed, but they can be.)
- There’s no `insert`method; insertion must be through either`insert_overwrite`or`insert_unique`. You must pick an insertion behavior.
- For hash maps, the default hasher is `foldhash`*not provide the same level of HashDoS resistance*as SipHash. If that is important to you, you can use a different hasher. (Disable the`default-hasher`feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed in.)
- The serde implementations reject duplicate keys.

We’ve also sometimes needed to index a set of data by more than one key, or
perhaps map one key to another. For that purpose, this crate provides
[ BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.7/iddqd/bi_hash_map/imp/struct.BiHashMap.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.7/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp/struct.TriHashMap.html)

`TriHashMap`- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

As a consequence of the general API structure, maps can have arbitrary non-key data associated with them as well.

### Examples

An example for [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.7/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html):

```
use ;
// Implement IdOrdItem so the map knows how to get the key from the value.
let mut users = new;
// You must pick an insertion behavior. insert_unique returns an error if
// the key already exists.
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
// Lookup by name:
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// Iterate over users:
for user in &users
```
Keys don’t have to be borrowed from the value. For smaller `Copy` types,
it’s recommended that you use owned keys. Here’s an example of using
[ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.7/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) with a small integer key:

```
// ...
```
An example for [ IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.7/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp/struct.IdHashMap.html), showing a complex borrowed key. Here,
“complex” means that the key is not a reference itself, but a struct that
returns references to more than one field from the value.

```
use ;
// The key type is a borrowed form of the name and version. It needs to
// implement `Eq + Hash`.
// Create a new `IdHashMap` with the given artifacts. This uses the
// `id_hash_map!` macro that comes with iddqd.
let artifacts = id_hash_map! ;
// Look up artifacts by name and version.
assert_eq!;
```
For more examples, see the
[examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd/examples)
and [extended
examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples)
directories.

`Equivalent` and `Comparable`

An important feature of the standard library’s maps is that they allow any
borrowed form of the key type to be used for lookups; for example, a
`HashMap<String, T>` type can be looked up with a `&str` key. This is done
through the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait.

But the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait is a bit too restrictive for complex keys such as

`ArtifactKey` above, requiring workarounds such as [dynamic dispatch](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example). To address this, the crates.io ecosystem has standardized on the

[and](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html)

`Equivalent`[traits as generalizations of](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable``Borrow`. The map types in
this crate require these traits.For a key type `T::Key<'_>` and a lookup type `L`:

- The hash map types require `L: Hash + Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. Also,`L`must hash in the same way as`T::Key<'_>`. Typically, this is done by ensuring that enum variants and struct fields are in the same order[^proptest].
- `IdOrdMap`- `L: Comparable<T::Key<'_>>`, which in turn requires- `Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. (There’s no need for- `L`to implement- `Ord`or- `Eq`itself.)

[^proptest]: We recommend that you test this with e.g. a property-based
test: see [this
example](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example/blob/a6f17699/src/lib.rs#L233).

Continuing the `ArtifactKey` example from above, we can perform a lookup
using a key of this owned form:

```
use Equivalent;
// This is an owned form of ArtifactKey. The fields are in the same
// order as ArtifactKey's fields, so it hashes the same way.
// Now you can use OwnedArtifactKey to look up the artifact.
let owned_key = OwnedArtifactKey ;
assert_eq!;
```
There’s a blanket implementation of [ Equivalent](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html) and

[for](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable`[, so if your type already implements](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`[, there aren’t any extra steps to take.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`## Testing

This crate is validated through a combination of:

- Unit tests
- Property-based tests using a naive map as an oracle
- Chaos tests for several kinds of buggy `Eq`and`Ord`implementations
- Miri tests for unsafe code

If you see a gap in testing, new tests are welcome. Thank you!

## No-std compatibility

Most of this crate is no-std compatible, though [ alloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/index.html) is required.

The [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.7/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) type is not currently no-std compatible due to its use of a
thread-local. This thread-local is just a way to work around a limitation in
std’s

`BTreeMap` API, though. Either a custom B-Tree implementation, or a
platform-specific notion of thread locals, would suffice to make
[no-std compatible.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.7/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html)

`IdOrdMap`## Optional features

- `serde`: Enables serde support for all ID map types.- *Not enabled by default.*
- `schemars08`: Enables- `schemars`- [automatic replacement](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/blob/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples/typify-types.rs)through- `typify`- `dropshot`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `daft`: Enables- `daft`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `std`: Enables std support.- *Enabled by default.*
- `default-hasher`: Enables the- `DefaultHashBuilder`type. Disable this feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed into- `IdHashMap`- `BiHashMap`- `TriHashMap`- *Enabled by default.*
- `allocator-api2`: Enables support for custom allocators via the- `allocator_api2`- `bumpalo`) are supported. Custom allocators are not currently supported by- `IdOrdMap`.

## Related work

-
`bimap`
-
`multi_index_map``Clone`. In`iddqd`, we pick a somewhat different point in the design space, but we think`multi_index_map`is also great.
-
In general, this is similar to relational database records with indexes. For sufficiently complex use cases, consider an embedded database like [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/), or even a networked database like[PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/).`iddqd`is a good fit for simple in-memory caches of data stored in these databases.

## Minimum supported Rust version (MSRV)

This crate’s MSRV is **Rust 1.81**. In general we aim for 6 months of Rust
compatibility.

## What does iddqd mean?

The name `iddqd` is a reference to [a cheat
code](https://doomwiki.org/wiki/Doom_cheat_codes) in the classic video game
*Doom*. It has `id` in the name, and is short and memorable.

# iddqd 0.3.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/iddqd/0.3.4

# iddqd

Maps where keys are borrowed from values.

This crate consists of several map types, collectively called **ID maps**:

- `IdOrdMap`
- `IdHashMap`
- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

## Usage

- Pick your ID map type.
- Depending on the ID map type, implement `IdOrdItem``IdHashItem``BiHashItem``TriHashItem`
- Store values in the ID map type.

### Features

This crate was built out a practical need for map types, and addresses issues encountered using Rust’s default map types in practice at Oxide.

- Keys are retrieved from values, not stored separately from them. Separate storage has been a recurring pain point in our codebases: if keys are duplicated within values, it’s proven to be hard to maintain consistency between keys and values. This crate addresses that need.
- Keys may be borrowed from values, which allows for more flexible implementations. (They don’t have to be borrowed, but they can be.)
- There’s no `insert`method; insertion must be through either`insert_overwrite`or`insert_unique`. You must pick an insertion behavior.
- For hash maps, the default hasher is `foldhash`*not provide the same level of HashDoS resistance*as SipHash. If that is important to you, you can use a different hasher. (Disable the`default-hasher`feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed in.)
- The serde implementations reject duplicate keys.

We’ve also sometimes needed to index a set of data by more than one key, or
perhaps map one key to another. For that purpose, this crate provides
[ BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.4/iddqd/bi_hash_map/imp/struct.BiHashMap.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.4/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp/struct.TriHashMap.html)

`TriHashMap`- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

As a consequence of the general API structure, maps can have arbitrary non-key data associated with them as well.

### Examples

An example for [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.4/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html):

```
use ;
// Implement IdOrdItem so the map knows how to get the key from the value.
let mut users = new;
// You must pick an insertion behavior. insert_unique returns an error if
// the key already exists.
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
// Lookup by name:
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// Iterate over users:
for user in &users
```
Keys don’t have to be borrowed from the value. For smaller `Copy` types,
it’s recommended that you use owned keys. Here’s an example of using
[ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.4/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) with a small integer key:

```
// ...
```
An example for [ IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.4/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp/struct.IdHashMap.html), showing a complex borrowed key. Here,
“complex” means that the key is not a reference itself, but a struct that
returns references to more than one field from the value.

```
use ;
// The key type is a borrowed form of the name and version. It needs to
// implement `Eq + Hash`.
let mut artifacts = new;
// Add artifacts to the map.
artifacts
    .insert_unique
    .unwrap;
artifacts
    .insert_unique
    .unwrap;
// Look up artifacts by name and version.
assert_eq!;
```
For more examples, see the
[examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd/examples)
and [extended
examples](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/iddqd/tree/main/crates/iddqd-extended-examples/examples)
directories.

`Equivalent` and `Comparable`

An important feature of the standard library’s maps is that they allow any
borrowed form of the key type to be used for lookups; for example, a
`HashMap<String, T>` type can be looked up with a `&str` key. This is done
through the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait.

But the [ Borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html) trait is a bit too restrictive for complex keys such as

`ArtifactKey` above, requiring workarounds such as [dynamic dispatch](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example). To address this, the crates.io ecosystem has standardized on the

[and](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html)

`Equivalent`[traits as generalizations of](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable``Borrow`. The map types in
this crate require these traits.For a key type `T::Key<'_>` and a lookup type `L`:

- The hash map types require `L: Hash + Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. Also,`L`must hash in the same way as`T::Key<'_>`. Typically, this is done by ensuring that enum variants and struct fields are in the same order[^proptest].
- `IdOrdMap`- `L: Comparable<T::Key<'_>>`, which in turn requires- `Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. (There’s no need for- `L`to implement- `Ord`or- `Eq`itself.)

[^proptest]: We recommend that you test this with e.g. a property-based
test: see [this
example](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example/blob/a6f17699/src/lib.rs#L233).

Continuing the `ArtifactKey` example from above, we can perform a lookup
using a key of this owned form:

```
use Equivalent;
// This is an owned form of ArtifactKey. The fields are in the same
// order as ArtifactKey's fields, so it hashes the same way.
// Now you can use OwnedArtifactKey to look up the artifact.
let owned_key = OwnedArtifactKey ;
assert_eq!;
```
There’s a blanket implementation of [ Equivalent](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html) and

[for](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable`[, so if your type already implements](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`[, there aren’t any extra steps to take.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`## Testing

This crate is validated through a combination of:

- Unit tests
- Property-based tests using a naive map as an oracle
- Chaos tests for several kinds of buggy `Eq`and`Ord`implementations
- Miri tests for unsafe code

If you see a gap in testing, new tests are welcome. Thank you!

## No-std compatibility

Most of this crate is no-std compatible, though [ alloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/index.html) is required.

The [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.4/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) type is not currently no-std compatible due to its use of a
thread-local. This thread-local is just a way to work around a limitation in
std’s

`BTreeMap` API, though. Either a custom B-Tree implementation, or a
platform-specific notion of thread locals, would suffice to make
[no-std compatible.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.4/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html)

`IdOrdMap`## Optional features

- `serde`: Enables serde support for all ID map types.- *Not enabled by default.*
- `daft`: Enables- `daft`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `std`: Enables std support.- *Enabled by default.*
- `default-hasher`: Enables the- `DefaultHashBuilder`type. Disable this feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed into- `IdHashMap`- `BiHashMap`- `TriHashMap`- *Enabled by default.*
- `allocator-api2`: Enables support for custom allocators via the- `allocator_api2`- `bumpalo`) are supported. Custom allocators are not currently supported by- `IdOrdMap`.

## Related work

-
`bimap`
-
`multi_index_map``Clone`. In`iddqd`, we pick a somewhat different point in the design space, but we think`multi_index_map`is also great.
-
In general, this is similar to relational database records with indexes. For sufficiently complex use cases, consider an embedded database like [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/), or even a networked database like[PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/).`iddqd`is a good fit for simple in-memory caches of data stored in these databases.

- `IdOrdMap`- `L: Comparable<T::Key<'_>>`, which in turn requires- `Equivalent<T::Key<'_>>`. (There’s no need for- `L`to implement- `Ord`or- `Eq`itself.)

[^proptest]: We recommend that you test this with e.g. a property-based
test: see [this
example](https://github.com/sunshowers-code/borrow-complex-key-example/blob/a6f17699/src/lib.rs#L233).

Continuing the `ArtifactKey` example from above, we can perform a lookup
using a key of this owned form:

```
use Equivalent;
// This is an owned form of ArtifactKey. The fields are in the same
// order as ArtifactKey's fields, so it hashes the same way.
// Now you can use OwnedArtifactKey to look up the artifact.
let owned_key = OwnedArtifactKey ;
assert_eq!;
```
There’s a blanket implementation of [ Equivalent](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Equivalent.html) and

[for](https://docs.rs/equivalent/1.0.2/equivalent/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable`[, so if your type already implements](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`[, there aren’t any extra steps to take.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html)

`Borrow`## Testing

This crate is validated through a combination of:

- Unit tests
- Property-based tests using a naive map as an oracle
- Chaos tests for several kinds of buggy `Eq`and`Ord`implementations
- Miri tests for unsafe code

If you see a gap in testing, new tests are welcome. Thank you!

## No-std compatibility

Most of this crate is no-std compatible, though [ alloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/index.html) is required.

The [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.2/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) type is not currently no-std compatible due to its use of a
thread-local. This thread-local is just a way to work around a limitation in
std’s

`BTreeMap` API, though. Either a custom B-Tree implementation, or a
platform-specific notion of thread locals, would suffice to make
[no-std compatible.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.2/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html)

`IdOrdMap`## Optional features

- `serde`: Enables serde support for all ID map types.- *Not enabled by default.*
- `daft`: Enables- `daft`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `std`: Enables std support.- *Enabled by default.*
- `default-hasher`: Enables the- `DefaultHashBuilder`type. Disable this feature to require a hash builder type parameter to be passed into- `IdHashMap`- `BiHashMap`- `TriHashMap`- *Enabled by default.*
- `allocator-api2`: Enables support for custom allocators via the- `allocator_api2`- `bumpalo`) are supported. Custom allocators are not currently supported by- `IdOrdMap`.

- `multi_index_map`- `Clone`. In- `iddqd`, we pick a somewhat different point in the design space, but we think- `multi_index_map`is also great.

# iddqd

Maps where keys are borrowed from values.

This crate consists of several map types, collectively called **ID maps**:

- `IdOrdMap`
- `IdHashMap`
- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

## Usage

- Pick your ID map type.
- Depending on the ID map type, implement `IdOrdItem``IdHashItem``BiHashItem``TriHashItem`
- Store values in the ID map type.

### Features

This crate was built out a practical need for map types, and addresses issues encountered using Rust’s default map types in practice at Oxide.

- Keys are retrieved from values, not stored separately from them. Separate storage has been a recurring pain point in our codebases: if keys are duplicated within values, it’s proven to be hard to maintain consistency between keys and values. This crate addresses that need.
- Keys may be borrowed from values, which allows for more flexible implementations. (They don’t have to be borrowed, but they can be.)
- There’s no `insert`method; insertion must be through either`insert_overwrite`or`insert_unique`. You must pick an insertion behavior.
- The serde implementations reject duplicate keys.

We’ve also sometimes needed to index a set of data by more than one key, or
perhaps map one key to another. For that purpose, this crate provides
[ BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.1/iddqd/bi_hash_map/imp/struct.BiHashMap.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.1/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp/struct.TriHashMap.html)

`TriHashMap`- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

As a consequence of the general API structure, maps can have arbitrary non-key data associated with them as well.

### Examples

An example for [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.1/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html):

```
use ;
// Implement IdOrdItem so the map knows how to get the key from the value.
let mut users = new;
// You must pick an insertion behavior. insert_unique returns an error if
// the key already exists.
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
// Lookup by name:
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// Iterate over users:
for user in &users
```
An example for [ IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.1/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp/struct.IdHashMap.html), showing complex borrowed keys.

```
use ;
// The key type is a borrowed form of the name and version. It needs to
// implement `Hash + Eq`.
let mut artifacts = new;
// Add artifacts to the map.
artifacts.insert_unique
.unwrap;
artifacts.insert_unique
.unwrap;
// Look up artifacts by name and version.
assert_eq!;
```
## Testing

This crate is validated through a combination of:

- Unit tests
- Property-based tests using a naive map as an oracle
- Chaos tests for several kinds of buggy `Eq`and`Ord`implementations
- Miri tests for unsafe code

If you see a gap in testing, new tests are welcome. Thank you!

## No-std compatibility

Most of this crate is no-std compatible, though [ alloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/index.html) is required.

The [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.1/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) type is not currently no-std compatible due to its use of a
thread-local. This thread-local is just a way to work around a limitation in
std’s

`BTreeMap` API, though. Either a custom B-Tree implementation, or a
platform-specific notion of thread locals, would suffice to make
[no-std compatible.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.3.1/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html)

`IdOrdMap`## Optional features

- `serde`: Enables serde support for all ID map types.- *Not enabled by default.*
- `daft`: Enables- `daft`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `std`: Enables std support.- *Enabled by default.*

## Related work

- `bimap`
- `multi_index_map`- `Clone`. In- `iddqd`, we pick a somewhat different point in the design space, but we think- `multi_index_map`is also great.

# iddqd 0.1.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/iddqd/0.1.1

# iddqd

Maps where keys are borrowed from values.

This crate consists of several map types, collectively called **ID maps**:

- `IdOrdMap`
- `IdHashMap`
- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

## Usage

- Pick your ID map type.
- Depending on the ID map type, implement `IdOrdItem``IdHashItem``BiHashItem``TriHashItem`
- Store values in the ID map type.

### Features

This crate was built out a practical need for map types, and addresses issues encountered using Rust’s default map types in practice at Oxide.

- Keys are retrieved from values, not stored separately from them. Separate storage has been a recurring pain point in our codebases: if keys are duplicated within values, it’s proven to be hard to maintain consistency between keys and values. This crate addresses that need.
- Keys may be borrowed from values, which allows for more flexible implementations. (They don’t have to be borrowed, but they can be.)
- There’s no `insert`method; insertion must be through either`insert_overwrite`or`insert_unique`. You must pick an insertion behavior.
- The serde implementations reject duplicate keys.

We’ve also sometimes needed to index a set of data by more than one key, or
perhaps map one key to another. For that purpose, this crate provides
[ BiHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.1.1/iddqd/bi_hash_map/imp/struct.BiHashMap.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.1.1/iddqd/tri_hash_map/imp/struct.TriHashMap.html)

`TriHashMap`- `BiHashMap`
- `TriHashMap`

As a consequence of the general API structure, maps can have arbitrary non-key data associated with them as well.

### Examples

An example for [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.1.1/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html):

```
use ;
// Implement IdOrdItem so the map knows how to get the key from the value.
let mut users = new;
// You must pick an insertion behavior. insert_unique returns an error if
// the key already exists.
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
users.insert_unique.unwrap;
// Lookup by name:
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// Iterate over users:
for user in &users
```
An example for [ IdHashMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.1.1/iddqd/id_hash_map/imp/struct.IdHashMap.html), showing complex borrowed keys.

```
use ;
// The key type is a borrowed form of the name and version. It needs to
// implement `Hash + Eq`.
let mut artifacts = new;
// Add artifacts to the map.
artifacts.insert_unique
.unwrap;
artifacts.insert_unique
.unwrap;
// Look up artifacts by name and version.
assert_eq!;
```
## Testing

This crate is validated through a combination of:

- Unit tests
- Property-based tests using a naive map as an oracle
- Chaos tests for several kinds of buggy `Eq`and`Ord`implementations
- Miri tests for unsafe code

If you see a gap in testing, new tests are welcome. Thank you!

## No-std compatibility

Most of this crate is no-std compatible, though [ alloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/index.html) is required.

The [ IdOrdMap](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.1.1/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html) type is not currently no-std compatible due to its use of a
thread-local. This thread-local is just a way to work around a limitation in
std’s

`BTreeMap` API, though. Either a custom B-Tree implementation, or a
platform-specific notion of thread locals, would suffice to make
[no-std compatible.](https://docs.rs/iddqd/0.1.1/iddqd/id_ord_map/imp/struct.IdOrdMap.html)

`IdOrdMap`## Optional features

- `serde`: Enables serde support for all ID map types.- *Not enabled by default.*
- `daft`: Enables- `daft`- *Not enabled by default.*
- `std`: Enables std support.- *Enabled by default.*

## Related work

- `bimap`

## Minimum supported Rust version (MSRV)

This crate’s MSRV is **Rust 1.81**. In general we aim for 6 months of Rust
compatibility.
